about: A shared UK-wide revision pack on gross anatomy and embryology, not one university's syllabus. It is used alongside preclinical anatomy modules at several UK medical schools and for anatomy revision in later years. It works region by region (back, thorax, abdomen, pelvis and perineum, upper and lower limb, head and neck), then covers early development and organ formation, always linking structure to clinical signs, procedures and imaging. Clinical anatomy sits in the biomedical sciences domain of the GMC's MLA content map, and many of the conditions used as examples here (cauda equina syndrome, pneumothorax, hernias, peripheral nerve palsies, Bell palsy, extradural haemorrhage, congenital heart disease) appear on that map. This is educational material, not clinical advice, and it gives no drug doses.

notes.h: Anatomical language, the vertebral column and the back
notes.overview: Every anatomical description assumes the anatomical position and a shared set of planes and terms. The vertebral column protects the spinal cord, carries body weight and lets the trunk move. Knowing how nerve roots leave the canal, where the cord ends and which root a disc compresses explains sciatica, lumbar puncture and cauda equina syndrome.
objectives: Describe the anatomical position and use planes, directional terms and movements correctly.
Explain why the cervical and lumbar curvatures are secondary while the thoracic and sacral curvatures are primary.
Predict which nerve root a posterolateral lumbar disc prolapse compresses and interpret the resulting signs.
Explain why lumbar puncture is performed below the level of the conus medullaris and name the layers crossed.
Recognise the red-flag features of suspected cauda equina syndrome and the urgency they demand.

sections.body:
All descriptions assume the anatomical position: standing upright, facing forwards, arms by the sides with the palms forward and the feet together.
- Sagittal plane: divides left from right (the median plane is the midline sagittal plane).
- Coronal (frontal) plane: divides front from back.
- Transverse (axial) plane: divides upper from lower (axial CT slices).
- Medial/lateral: nearer to or further from the midline. Proximal/distal: nearer to or further from the root of a limb.
- Movements come in pairs: flexion and extension, abduction (away from the midline) and adduction, medial and lateral rotation, pronation and supination (forearm), inversion and eversion, and dorsiflexion and plantarflexion (foot).

sections.h: Vertebrae, curvatures, discs and nerve roots
sections.body:
The column usually has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar vertebrae, a sacrum of 5 fused vertebrae and a small coccyx. A typical vertebra has a body in front and an arch (pedicles and laminae) behind, enclosing the vertebral foramen.
- The thoracic and sacral kyphoses are primary curvatures, present before birth. The cervical and lumbar lordoses are secondary, developing as the infant holds up its head and then stands and walks.
- Each intervertebral disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus and a gel-like central nucleus pulposus. Herniation is usually posterolateral, where the posterior longitudinal ligament gives least support.
- The anterior longitudinal ligament limits hyperextension; the posterior longitudinal ligament limits hyperflexion; the elastic ligamentum flavum joins adjacent laminae.
- Root numbering: C1–C7 roots leave above the vertebra of the same number, C8 leaves between C7 and T1, and from T1 downwards each root leaves below its own vertebra.

In the lumbar spine each root runs down the canal before leaving through its foramen under the pedicle. A posterolateral prolapse at L4/L5 therefore usually compresses the traversing L5 root, not the exiting L4 root, which has already left above the disc. A far-lateral prolapse can catch the exiting root instead.
Typical root patterns (they overlap):
- L4: weak knee extension, reduced knee jerk, numbness over the medial leg and ankle.
- L5: weak big-toe extension and ankle dorsiflexion, numbness over the dorsum of the foot and big toe; reflexes are often normal.
- S1: weak plantarflexion (difficulty standing on tiptoe), reduced or absent ankle jerk, numbness over the lateral foot.
The knee jerk tests mainly L3–L4 and the ankle jerk S1. Dermatomal pain below the knee with a positive straight-leg raise suggests root irritation (sciatica). The intrinsic back muscles (erector spinae: iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis from lateral to medial) are supplied by posterior rami; the extrinsic muscles (trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids) move the upper limb.

In adults the spinal cord ends as the conus medullaris at about L1/L2 (TeachMeAnatomy gives the L2 level); below this the subarachnoid space widens into the lumbar cistern, which contains CSF and the roots of the cauda equina. The dural sac continues to about S2.
- Lumbar puncture is therefore done at L3/L4 or L4/L5, where the needle meets floating nerve roots rather than the cord. The line joining the highest points of the iliac crests (Tuffier's or the supracristal line) is used to find the L4 level or the L4/L5 interspace, but it is an imprecise landmark.
- In the midline the needle crosses skin, subcutaneous tissue, the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, the ligamentum flavum (a distinct 'give'), the epidural space, the dura and the arachnoid, and then reaches CSF in the subarachnoid space.
- MRI shows discs, roots and the cauda equina; plain X-rays show bone but not a disc prolapse.

sections.h: Suspected cauda equina syndrome (current England pathway)

sections.body:
A 42-year-old develops back pain while lifting, then pain down the back of the left thigh to the outer foot; straight-leg raising reproduces it. Plantarflexion is weak, the left ankle jerk is absent and pinprick is reduced along the lateral border of the foot. Saddle sensation and bladder function are normal.
The pattern points to the S1 root. At L5/S1 the L5 root has already left above the disc, so a posterolateral L5/S1 prolapse catches the traversing S1 root. The ankle-jerk arc runs through S1, and gastrocnemius and soleus are supplied mainly by S1–S2 through the tibial nerve. With no red flags he does not need emergency imaging, but he is told which symptoms (saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, weakness in both legs) mean attending hospital at once.

- Students often think an L4/L5 prolapse compresses L4. In fact a posterolateral prolapse usually catches the traversing L5 root, because L4 has already left through the foramen above the disc.
- Students often think lumbar puncture is done at L1/L2 'because that is where the lumbar spine starts'. In fact the cord may end at that level, so the needle goes lower, at L3/L4 or L4/L5.
- Students often think a normal bladder scan rules out cauda equina syndrome. In fact the pathway says a bladder scan must not decide on MRI alone.

notes.h: Thorax: wall, pleura, lungs, mediastinum and heart
notes.overview: The thorax packs the lungs and heart inside a moving cage of ribs and muscle. Surface landmarks such as the sternal angle, the costal groove and the pleural reflections guide chest drains and examination, and coronary anatomy explains which part of the heart, and which part of the conducting system, suffers when a particular artery blocks.
objectives: Use the sternal angle and rib counting to locate thoracic structures and levels.
Explain why chest drains and needles pass just above a rib within the triangle of safety.
Distinguish parietal from visceral pleura by nerve supply and explain referred shoulder-tip pain.
Interpret the signs of tension pneumothorax in terms of pleural and mediastinal anatomy.
Predict the territory and conduction problems caused by occlusion of each coronary artery.

sections.h: Chest wall, landmarks and the diaphragm
sections.body:
Ribs 1–7 reach the sternum by their own cartilage; 8–10 join the cartilage above; 11–12 float. The sternal angle (manubriosternal joint) is where the second costal cartilage joins, so rib counting starts there. A plane from the sternal angle to about the T4/T5 disc separates the superior from the inferior mediastinum; at this level the aortic arch begins and ends, the trachea divides and the azygos vein joins the superior vena cava.
- Each intercostal space has external, internal and innermost intercostal muscles. The neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above down) runs in the costal groove under the rib above, between the internal and innermost layers.
- The diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3–C5) has three main openings: the IVC at T8 (with branches of the right phrenic nerve), the oesophagus at T10 (with the vagal trunks) and the aorta at T12 (with the thoracic duct and azygos vein).

Parietal pleura lines the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum; visceral pleura covers the lung. Parietal pleura is supplied by the intercostal and phrenic nerves and is sensitive to pain, so pleurisy gives sharp, well-localised pain. Visceral pleura has only autonomic supply and senses stretch, not pain.
- Pain from the central diaphragmatic pleura travels in the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) and is felt at the shoulder tip, because C4 also supplies the skin there.
- Lungs: the right has three lobes (horizontal and oblique fissures), the left two, with a cardiac notch and lingula. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled objects usually go right.
- Surface markings (approximate): the lower lung border crosses ribs 6, 8 and 10 at the midclavicular, midaxillary and paravertebral lines; the pleura lies about two ribs lower (8, 10, 12), leaving the costodiaphragmatic recess where effusions collect.
- The phrenic nerves pass in front of the lung roots and the vagi behind. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum.

The right atrium forms the right heart border, the left ventricle most of the left border and apex, the right ventricle most of the anterior surface and the left atrium most of the posterior surface (base).
- Right coronary artery: runs in the right atrioventricular groove, supplying the right atrium, most of the right ventricle and, through its branches, the SA node in most people and the AV node in right-dominant hearts.
- Left coronary artery: divides into the left anterior descending artery (anterior left ventricle and anterior two-thirds of the septum) and the circumflex (lateral and posterior left ventricle, left atrium).
- Dominance is defined by which artery gives the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery. This is the right coronary artery in most people (about 80–85%), so the RCA usually supplies the inferior wall and posterior third of the septum.

sections.h: Reading the chest: examination, imaging and ECG territories
sections.body:
- Basal dullness suggests fluid in the costodiaphragmatic recess; hyperresonance with absent breath sounds suggests pleural air.
- On a chest X-ray the right heart border is the right atrium; loss of the right heart border suggests disease in the adjacent right middle lobe, and loss of a hemidiaphragm outline suggests lower lobe disease.
- ECG leads look at territories: II, III and aVF view the inferior wall (usually the RCA); V1–V4 the septum and anterior wall (LAD); I, aVL, V5 and V6 the lateral wall (circumflex or diagonal branches).
- Ultrasound shows where pleural fluid, diaphragm and organs lie.

sections.h: Chest drains and decompression: anatomical safety
sections.body:
The BTS clinical statement on pleural procedures (2023) advises insertion within the triangle of safety and directly above a rib, to avoid the intercostal vessels; posterior approaches are avoided because the bundle is less protected there. Ultrasound guidance is expected for pleural fluid procedures except in emergencies, large-bore drains are inserted by blunt dissection, and sharp trocars are advised against.
- The triangle of safety is bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a horizontal line at about the fifth intercostal space, with its apex below the axilla.
- Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: an unstable patient is decompressed before imaging. StatPearls describes the second intercostal space in the midclavicular line and, when time permits, the fifth space at the anterior axillary line, which it reports has higher success and fewer complications. A chest drain follows decompression.
- At risk: intercostal vessels, the long thoracic nerve behind the triangle, and liver or spleen if too low.

A 23-year-old is stabbed in the left chest. He is breathless and hypotensive, his trachea is deviated to the right, the left chest is hyperresonant with absent breath sounds and his neck veins are distended. The wound has acted as a one-way valve, so air enters the pleural space on each breath but cannot escape. Rising pressure collapses the left lung and pushes the mediastinum to the right; kinking of the great veins reduces venous return, so the neck veins fill and cardiac output falls. The diagnosis is clinical, so he is decompressed at once and a chest drain is then placed in the triangle of safety, just above the upper border of a rib so the needle and tube pass below the neurovascular bundle of the space.

- Students often place the neurovascular bundle on the upper border of the rib. In fact it runs in the costal groove under the lower border, so needles go just above the rib below.
- Students often think the left ventricle forms the front of the heart. In fact the right ventricle forms most of the anterior surface; the left ventricle forms the apex and left border.
- Students often think coronary dominance means the larger artery. It is defined by which artery gives the posterior interventricular artery.
- Students often confuse lung and pleural levels: the pleura extends about two ribs lower.

- Basal dullness suggests fluid in the costodiaphragmatic recess; hyperresonance with absent breath sounds suggests pleural air.

- ECG leads look at territories: II, III and aVF view the inferior wall (usually the RCA); V1–V4 the septum and anterior wall (LAD); I, aVL, V5 and V6 the lateral wall (circumflex or diagonal branches).

The BTS clinical statement on pleural procedures (2023) advises insertion within the triangle of safety and directly above a rib, to avoid the intercostal vessels; posterior approaches are avoided because the bundle is less protected there. - The triangle of safety is bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a horizontal line at about the fifth intercostal space, with its apex below the axilla.

A 23-year-old is stabbed in the left chest. sections.body:

- Femoral hernia: passes through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament, appearing below and lateral to the pubic tubercle; the narrow neck makes strangulation more likely.
- Calot's triangle (cystic duct, common hepatic duct, inferior surface of the liver) contains the cystic artery, usually from the right hepatic artery, and the cystic lymph node (of Lund).
- The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas from the splenic and superior mesenteric veins. Portosystemic anastomoses lie at the lower oesophagus, anorectum, umbilicus (paraumbilical veins) and retroperitoneum; in portal hypertension they dilate into varices.

notes.overview: The pelvis transmits weight to the legs, supports the pelvic organs through the pelvic floor and contains the lower gut, bladder and reproductive organs. Nerve supply, lymphatic drainage and the pectinate line explain why pelvic conditions hurt (or do not), where cancers spread and what is at risk in childbirth and surgery.
objectives: Describe the pelvic floor and perineum and the course and branches of the pudendal nerve.

sections.h: Bony pelvis, pelvic floor and perineum
sections.body:
The bony pelvis is formed by the two hip bones (ilium, ischium and pubis, fused at the acetabulum), the sacrum and the coccyx. The typical female pelvis has a wider, more oval inlet, a wider subpubic angle and a larger outlet than the male, suiting childbirth.
- Pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm): levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus. It supports the pelvic organs and, through puborectalis looping around the anorectal junction, maintains the anorectal angle that helps faecal continence.
- Perineum: the diamond-shaped region below the pelvic floor. A line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind.
- Perineal body: a central fibromuscular anchor for perineal muscles; tears or episiotomy here can extend towards the anal sphincter.

The pudendal nerve (S2–S4) leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, crosses the sacrospinous ligament close to the ischial spine and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal canal.
- Branches: the inferior rectal nerve (external anal sphincter and perianal skin), the perineal nerve (perineal muscles, external urethral sphincter, perineal skin) and the dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris.
- The ischial spine, felt through the vaginal wall, is the landmark for a pudendal nerve block; the nerve runs with the internal pudendal vessels, so aspiration precedes injection.
- Bladder: parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) contract the detrusor to empty the bladder; sympathetic fibres (from about T11–L2) relax the detrusor and close the bladder neck during filling; the pudendal nerve gives voluntary control of the external urethral sphincter.
- Sexual function: erection is mainly parasympathetic, emission sympathetic, and ejaculation needs rhythmic somatic contraction of bulbospongiosus via the pudendal nerve.

sections.h: The anal canal and the pectinate line
sections.body:
The pectinate line marks the junction of hindgut endoderm above and ectoderm (proctodeum) below, so supply changes across it.
- Above: columnar epithelium; superior rectal artery (from the inferior mesenteric); superior rectal vein to the portal system; lymph to internal iliac (and inferior mesenteric) nodes; visceral nerves, sensitive to stretch but not to pain.
- Below: stratified squamous epithelium; inferior rectal artery (from the internal pudendal); inferior rectal vein to the systemic system; lymph to superficial inguinal nodes; somatic inferior rectal nerves, sensitive to pain, touch and temperature.
- Internal anal sphincter: involuntary smooth muscle. External anal sphincter: voluntary skeletal muscle supplied by the inferior rectal nerve.
Internal haemorrhoids arise above the line and are typically painless; lesions below the line, such as an anal fissure or thrombosed external haemorrhoid, hurt.

- Digital rectal examination feels structures in front of the rectum: the prostate in men (its posterior peripheral zone, where most prostate cancers arise) and the cervix and rectouterine pouch in women.

notes.h: Upper limb: brachial plexus, nerve injuries and key regions
notes.overview: Most upper limb exam questions turn on one skill: knowing which nerve supplies which muscle and patch of skin, and where along its course it is injured. The brachial plexus, the named nerves and a handful of regions (axilla, cubital fossa, carpal tunnel, anatomical snuffbox) explain common fractures, palsies and entrapments.
objectives: Describe the organisation of the brachial plexus and the branches of each cord.
Predict the deficits after injury to the axillary, radial, median, ulnar, musculocutaneous and long thoracic nerves.
Distinguish upper (Erb) from lower (Klumpke) brachial plexus injury.
Explain the anatomy behind carpal tunnel syndrome and the ulnar paradox.
Interpret upper limb myotome and reflex findings to localise a root lesion.

sections.body:
The brachial plexus forms from the anterior rami of C5–T1 and is organised as roots, trunks, divisions, cords and branches. The roots pass between scalenus anterior and medius; the cords are named by their position around the axillary artery.
- Roots: dorsal scapular nerve (C5, rhomboids) and long thoracic nerve (C5–C7, serratus anterior).
- Trunks: upper (C5–C6), middle (C7), lower (C8–T1). The upper trunk gives the suprascapular nerve (supraspinatus, infraspinatus).
- Lateral cord: musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve.
- Medial cord: ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve.
- Posterior cord: upper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves.
Rotator cuff: supraspinatus starts abduction (first 0–15°) and deltoid (axillary nerve) continues it; infraspinatus and teres minor (axillary nerve) laterally rotate; subscapularis (subscapular nerves) medially rotates. Trapezius and serratus anterior rotate the scapula for abduction above about 90°.

Traction that widens the angle between neck and shoulder stretches the upper roots; traction on an abducted arm stretches the lower roots.
- Erb palsy (C5–C6): loss of shoulder abduction and lateral rotation, elbow flexion and supination. The arm hangs adducted and medially rotated with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated ('waiter's tip'). Causes include difficult deliveries and motorcycle falls on the shoulder.
- Klumpke palsy (C8–T1): weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles with clawing, and sensory loss along the medial forearm and hand. If the T1 root is avulsed near the cord, sympathetic fibres to the head are interrupted, producing Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).
- Long thoracic nerve injury (for example during axillary surgery) paralyses serratus anterior, so the scapula wings when the patient pushes against a wall.

- Axillary nerve (surgical neck fracture, anterior shoulder dislocation): weak deltoid and numbness over the 'regimental badge' area of the upper lateral arm.
- Radial nerve in the radial groove (midshaft humeral fracture): wrist drop and numbness over the dorsum of the hand near the first web space. Triceps is weakened but not paralysed, because branches to its long and lateral heads leave above the groove.
- Median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome): numbness and tingling of the palmar lateral three and a half digits, often worse at night; later thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction. Thenar skin is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum.
- Ulnar nerve: weak finger abduction and adduction, interosseous wasting, a positive Froment's sign (thumb adduction lost) and clawing of the ring and little fingers. In the 'ulnar paradox' a wrist lesion claws more than an elbow lesion, because an elbow lesion also paralyses the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus, so the fingers are pulled into flexion less.
- Musculocutaneous nerve: weak elbow flexion and supination and numbness of the lateral forearm.

A structured neurological examination localises lesions to a root, plexus or peripheral nerve.
- Myotomes: shoulder abduction C5; elbow flexion C5/6; wrist extension C6; elbow and finger extension C7; finger abduction and thumb abduction T1.
- Reflexes: biceps C5/6, supinator (brachioradialis) C5/6, triceps C7.
- Dermatomes: C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial forearm.
- Special tests: Tinel's sign (tapping over the median nerve at the wrist) and Phalen's manoeuvre (sustained wrist flexion) reproduce carpal tunnel symptoms; Froment's sign tests adductor pollicis (ulnar). Nerve conduction studies confirm an entrapment and its level.

A 25-year-old motorcyclist lands on his right shoulder with his head forced to the left. His right arm hangs by his side, adducted and medially rotated, with the elbow extended and forearm pronated. The brachial plexus
The brachial plexus forms from the anterior rami of C5–T1 and is organised as roots, trunks, divisions, cords and branches. The roots pass between scalenus anterior and medius; the cords are named by their position around the axillary artery.
- Roots: dorsal scapular nerve (C5, rhomboids) and long thoracic nerve (C5–C7, serratus anterior).
- Trunks: upper (C5–C6), middle (C7), lower (C8–T1). The upper trunk gives the suprascapular nerve (supraspinatus, infraspinatus).
- Lateral cord: musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve.
- Medial cord: ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve.
- Posterior cord: upper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves.
Rotator cuff: supraspinatus starts abduction (first 0–15°) and deltoid (axillary nerve) continues it; infraspinatus and teres minor (axillary nerve) laterally rotate; subscapularis (subscapular nerves) medially rotates. Trapezius and serratus anterior rotate the scapula for abduction above about 90°.

Plexus injuries
Traction that widens the angle between neck and shoulder stretches the upper roots; traction on an abducted arm stretches the lower roots.
- Erb palsy (C5–C6): loss of shoulder abduction and lateral rotation, elbow flexion and supination. The arm hangs adducted and medially rotated with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated ('waiter's tip'). Causes include difficult deliveries and motorcycle falls on the shoulder.
- Klumpke palsy (C8–T1): weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles with clawing, and sensory loss along the medial forearm and hand. If the T1 root is avulsed near the cord, sympathetic fibres to the head are interrupted, producing Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).
- Long thoracic nerve injury (for example during axillary surgery) paralyses serratus anterior, so the scapula wings when the patient pushes against a wall.

- Axillary nerve (surgical neck fracture, anterior shoulder dislocation): weak deltoid and numbness over the 'regimental badge' area of the upper lateral arm.
- Radial nerve in the radial groove (midshaft humeral fracture): wrist drop and numbness over the dorsum of the hand near the first web space. Triceps is weakened but not paralysed, because branches to its long and lateral heads leave above the groove.
- Median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome): numbness and tingling of the palmar lateral three and a half digits, often worse at night; later thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction. Thenar skin is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum.

- Musculocutaneous nerve: weak elbow flexion and supination and numbness of the lateral forearm.

sections.h: Gait, hip abductors and the femoral head
sections.body:
When we stand on one leg, gluteus medius and minimus of the stance side hold the pelvis level. If they are weak or the superior gluteal nerve is injured, the pelvis drops on the opposite, unsupported side: a positive Trendelenburg sign, with a lurching gait.
The femoral head is supplied mainly by the medial circumflex femoral artery, whose retinacular branches run up the neck beneath the capsule's synovial reflection; the artery in the ligament of the head contributes little in adults. A displaced intracapsular neck fracture can tear these retinacular vessels, so the head is at risk of avascular necrosis and non-union. Extracapsular (trochanteric) fractures leave this supply intact. After a displaced neck fracture the leg is classically shortened and externally rotated, because muscles crossing the hip pull the shaft upwards and the lateral rotators and iliopsoas turn it outwards.

- Femoral triangle: inguinal ligament above, medial border of sartorius laterally, medial border of adductor longus medially. From lateral to medial it contains the femoral nerve, artery, vein and the femoral canal (lymphatics). The artery, vein and canal sit inside the femoral sheath; the nerve lies outside it. The femoral pulse is at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.
- Popliteal fossa: diamond bounded by biceps femoris, semimembranosus and semitendinosus, and the two heads of gastrocnemius. From superficial to deep: tibial nerve (with the common fibular nerve laterally), popliteal vein, popliteal artery. The artery is deepest, so its pulse is felt with the knee flexed.
- Knee: the anterior cruciate ligament stops the tibia sliding forwards on the femur (tested by the Lachman and anterior drawer tests); the posterior cruciate stops it sliding backwards. The medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament and capsule, so it is less mobile and often injured with the MCL.
- Ankle inversion sprains most often tear the anterior talofibular ligament.

- Dermatomes: L3 medial knee; L4 medial leg and ankle; L5 dorsum of foot and big toe; S1 lateral foot and little toe.

- Imaging: hip fractures are confirmed on X-ray (with MRI or CT if X-ray is normal but suspicion remains).

- Total hip replacement rather than hemiarthroplasty is considered for selected people, using criteria about pre-fracture independence, fitness for surgery and likely benefit beyond two years [2023].
- Trochanteric fractures above and including the lesser trochanter (except reverse oblique patterns): use an extramedullary implant such as a sliding hip screw in preference to an intramedullary nail [2011, amended 2023].
- Subtrochanteric fractures: use an intramedullary nail [2011].
The principle is that extracapsular fractures keep the head's blood supply and can be fixed, while displaced intracapsular fractures usually need the head replaced. Hip fracture surgery is otherwise outside the scope of this anatomy pack.

notes.overview: Head and neck anatomy is dense, but most clinical questions use a few ideas: what passes through each skull foramen, the courses of the cranial nerves (especially VII and the recurrent laryngeal branch of X), the meningeal layers in head injury, and the triangles and fascia of the neck that guide surgery and airway procedures.
objectives: Match the main skull foramina to the structures that pass through them.
Distinguish extradural from subdural haematoma by vessel, layer and CT appearance.

sections.body:
- Cribriform plate: olfactory nerve (I). Optic canal: optic nerve (II) and ophthalmic artery.
- Superior orbital fissure: III, IV, branches of V1 and VI, and the superior ophthalmic vein.
- Foramen rotundum: V2. Foramen ovale: V3. Foramen spinosum: middle meningeal artery.
- Internal acoustic meatus: VII and VIII. Jugular foramen: IX, X and XI with the internal jugular vein (from the sigmoid sinus). Hypoglossal canal: XII. Foramen magnum: medulla and vertebral arteries.
The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, enters through the foramen spinosum and runs between the skull and the dura. At the pterion, where frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet, the skull is thin and overlies a branch of this artery. An extradural haematoma lies between bone and dura; a subdural haematoma lies between dura and arachnoid, from torn bridging veins.

sections.h: Facial nerve and upper versus lower motor neuron weakness
sections.body:
The facial nerve leaves the brainstem, enters the internal acoustic meatus with VIII and runs through the facial canal in the temporal bone. At the geniculate ganglion it gives the greater petrosal nerve (lacrimal and nasal glands); further along it gives the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani (taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and secretomotor fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands). It leaves through the stylomastoid foramen and divides in the parotid into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches.
- Lower motor neuron lesion (e.g. Bell's palsy): the whole of one side of the face is weak, including the forehead.
- Upper motor neuron lesion (e.g. stroke): the forehead is relatively spared, because the motor neurons for the upper face receive input from both hemispheres; the lower face on the opposite side to the lesion is weak.
The branches that are affected localise a lower motor neuron lesion along the canal.

- Tongue: general sensation to the anterior two-thirds by the lingual nerve (V3) and taste by the chorda tympani (VII); both to the posterior third by IX. All tongue muscles are supplied by XII except palatoglossus (X). With a lower motor neuron XII lesion the protruded tongue deviates towards the weak side.
- Larynx: all intrinsic muscles are supplied by the recurrent (inferior) laryngeal nerve except cricothyroid, which tenses the cords and is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve. Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal folds. The cricoid cartilage (about C6) is the only complete ring; the cricothyroid membrane is the site for an emergency surgical airway.
- Neck triangles: the posterior triangle lies between sternocleidomastoid, trapezius and the middle third of the clavicle. The accessory nerve (XI) crosses it superficially, so it can be injured during lymph node biopsy, weakening trapezius.
- Carotid sheath: common or internal carotid artery medially, internal jugular vein laterally and the vagus between and behind them.

sections.h: Head injury and thyroid surgery: what tests show
sections.body:
- CT head: an extradural haematoma is typically biconvex (lens-shaped) and rarely crosses suture lines, because the dura is firmly attached at sutures. An acute subdural haematoma is crescent-shaped, follows the surface of the brain and can cross sutures. StatPearls quotes a classic lucid interval in only about 14–21% of people with an extradural haematoma, so its absence does not exclude one.
- Thyroid: the gland lies within the pretracheal fascia and moves on swallowing. It is supplied by the superior thyroid artery (external carotid) and the inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk); the recurrent laryngeal nerves lie in the tracheo-oesophageal grooves close to the inferior thyroid artery.
- After thyroidectomy, serum adjusted calcium is checked because the parathyroid glands, supplied mainly by the inferior thyroid artery, can be removed or devascularised. Voice change prompts laryngoscopy to look at vocal fold movement.

A 47-year-old wakes with drooping of the right side of his face. He cannot close his right eye or wrinkle his right forehead, sounds are unpleasantly loud in his right ear, food tastes odd on the right of his tongue and his right eye seems dry. Hearing is otherwise normal.

Normal hearing makes a cerebellopontine angle tumour, which would usually involve VIII, less likely. With no other cause found, this is Bell's palsy (listed on the GMC MLA content map). Protecting the eye, which cannot close, is an early practical priority.

notes.h: Embryology: early development and organ formation
notes.overview: Embryology explains adult anatomy: why nerves take strange routes, why the gut has three arteries, why the testis drains to the abdomen and why particular birth defects occur together. The key stages are gastrulation, neural tube formation, the fetal circulation and its changes at birth, the pharyngeal apparatus and rotation of the midgut.
objectives: Describe gastrulation and list major derivatives of ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.
Explain neural tube closure and the anatomical basis of anencephaly and spina bifida.
Explain how the fetal shunts work and what each becomes after birth.

sections.body:
The zygote divides to form a morula and then a blastocyst, with an inner cell mass (the future embryo) and an outer trophoblast (future placenta), which implants at about the end of the first week.
- Week 2: the inner cell mass becomes a bilaminar disc of epiblast and hypoblast, with the amniotic cavity and yolk sac; the trophoblast forms cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast.

Both cases show how a single developmental step explains a later presentation.

cards.f: Anatomical position
cards.b: Standing upright facing forwards, arms by the sides with palms facing forwards, feet together. All directional terms refer to this position.
cards.ex: Palms forwards is the detail most often forgotten; it is why the radius is 'lateral'.

cards.f: Sagittal vs coronal vs transverse plane
cards.b: Sagittal divides left from right (median = midline sagittal); coronal divides front from back; transverse (axial) divides upper from lower.
cards.ex: Think of the sagittal suture running front to back: a sagittal cut follows it.

cards.f: Why are the thoracic and sacral curvatures called primary?
cards.b: They are present before birth, keeping the fetal C-shaped flexion. The cervical and lumbar lordoses are secondary, appearing when the infant holds up its head and then stands and walks.
cards.ex: Primary = present first (fetal posture); secondary = acquired with posture.

cards.f: Which root does a posterolateral L4/L5 disc prolapse usually compress, and why?
cards.b: The traversing L5 root. L4 has already left through the foramen above the disc; L5 runs past the disc to leave below the L5 pedicle.
cards.ex: Lumbar roots leave below their own vertebra, so the disc lies below the exiting root's foramen.

cards.f: Absent ankle jerk, weak plantarflexion and numbness of the lateral foot: which root?
cards.b: S1, most often from a posterolateral L5/S1 disc prolapse.
cards.ex: The ankle jerk arc runs through S1; the lateral foot is the S1 dermatome.

cards.f: Anterior vs posterior longitudinal ligament
cards.b: Anterior: broad, on the front of the bodies and discs, limits hyperextension. Posterior: narrower, inside the canal on the back of the bodies, limits hyperflexion; its narrowness leaves the disc weak posterolaterally.
cards.ex: The posterior ligament's narrowness is why discs herniate posterolaterally.

cards.f: Why is lumbar puncture performed at L3/L4 or L4/L5?
cards.b: The adult cord ends at about L1/L2, so a needle below this enters the lumbar cistern, where nerve roots float in CSF and move aside rather than being pierced.
cards.ex: The dural sac goes on to about S2, so CSF is available well below the cord.

cards.f: Layers crossed by a midline lumbar puncture needle
cards.b: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura, arachnoid, then the subarachnoid space (CSF).
cards.ex: The 'give' felt on passing ligamentum flavum precedes the epidural space.

cards.f: Why does the C8 root break the numbering pattern?
cards.b: There are eight cervical roots but only seven cervical vertebrae. C1–C7 leave above their vertebra; C8 leaves between C7 and T1, so from T1 down each root leaves below its vertebra.
cards.ex: C8 is the 'switch-over' root.

cards.f: Sciatica plus new difficulty starting to pass urine and perianal numbness: what next?
cards.b: Suspect cauda equina syndrome: emergency referral to hospital for MRI as soon as possible (the England pathway asks for within four hours of request).
cards.ex: Sacral roots (S2–S5) carry bladder control and saddle sensation, so their compression is an emergency.

cards.f: Intrinsic vs extrinsic back muscles: nerve supply
cards.b: Intrinsic (erector spinae, transversospinalis) are supplied by posterior rami. Extrinsic (trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, levator scapulae) move the upper limb and are supplied by anterior rami or the accessory nerve.
cards.ex: Supply reflects origin: intrinsic muscles develop from the back's own segmental muscle.

cards.f: Structures and events at the sternal angle
cards.b: Second costal cartilage; boundary of superior and inferior mediastinum; start and end of the aortic arch; tracheal bifurcation; azygos vein joins the SVC. Level with about the T4/T5 disc.
cards.ex: Rib counting starts at the second cartilage beside the angle.

cards.f: Why are chest drains passed just over the upper border of a rib?
cards.b: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove under the lower border of each rib, so going over the rib below avoids the main bundle.
cards.ex: VAN sits under the rib above, between internal and innermost intercostals.

cards.f: Why is pain from the central diaphragm felt at the shoulder tip?
cards.b: Central diaphragmatic pleura and peritoneum are supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5); C4 also supplies shoulder skin, so the brain misattributes the pain.
cards.ex: Referred pain follows shared spinal segments.

cards.f: Parietal vs visceral pleura
cards.b: Parietal: intercostal and phrenic nerves, pain-sensitive, well localised. Visceral: autonomic supply, senses stretch only, not pain.
cards.ex: Pleuritic pain comes from the parietal layer.

cards.f: Why do inhaled foreign bodies usually go into the right lung?
cards.b: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so it continues more directly from the trachea.
cards.ex: Picture the carina: the right bronchus runs almost straight down.

cards.f: Hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, trachea deviated away, raised JVP, hypotension
cards.b: Tension pneumothorax on the hyperresonant side: air under pressure collapses the lung, shifts the mediastinum and impairs venous return.
cards.ex: Raised JVP plus hypotension shows the problem is venous return, not blood loss.

cards.f: Coronary dominance vs which artery is 'bigger'
cards.b: Dominance is defined by which artery gives the posterior interventricular artery: the RCA in most people (about 80–85%). Size is irrelevant.
cards.ex: Definition by origin of the posterior descending artery.

cards.f: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with sinus bradycardia in a right-dominant heart: which artery?
cards.b: Right coronary artery: it supplies the inferior wall in right dominance and usually the SA node, and in right dominance the AV node.
cards.ex: Inferior leads plus nodal dysfunction point to the RCA.

cards.f: Which chamber does a parasternal stab wound in the left fourth intercostal space enter first?
cards.b: The right ventricle, because it forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart.
cards.ex: The left ventricle lies further left and behind.

cards.f: Diaphragm openings and levels
cards.b: IVC at T8 (with right phrenic branches); oesophagus at T10 (with vagal trunks); aorta at T12 (with thoracic duct and azygos vein).
cards.ex: 'I 8 10 eggs at 12': IVC 8, oesophagus 10, aorta 12.

cards.f: Why can an enlarged left atrium or a left apical lung tumour cause hoarseness?
cards.b: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch and climbs back in the neck; pressure or invasion in the thorax weakens the left vocal fold.
cards.ex: The right nerve hooks under the subclavian in the neck, so it is spared by thoracic disease.

cards.f: Walls of the inguinal canal
cards.b: Anterior: external oblique aponeurosis (+ internal oblique laterally). Posterior: transversalis fascia (+ conjoint tendon medially). Roof: internal oblique and transversus. Floor: inguinal ligament.
cards.ex: MALT: Muscles (roof), Aponeuroses (anterior), Ligaments (floor), Tendon and transversalis (posterior).

cards.f: Direct vs indirect inguinal hernia
cards.b: Indirect: through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, along the processus vaginalis. Direct: through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the vessels, from wall weakness.
cards.ex: The inferior epigastric vessels are the dividing line.

cards.f: Inguinal vs femoral hernia by landmark
cards.b: Inguinal hernias emerge above and medial to the pubic tubercle; femoral hernias emerge below and lateral to it, through the femoral canal under the inguinal ligament.
cards.ex: Feel for the pubic tubercle first.

cards.f: Why is foregut pain felt in the epigastrium and midgut pain around the umbilicus?
cards.b: Visceral afferents return to the spinal segments that supplied each gut region in development; the brain projects that pain onto the matching midline skin.
cards.ex: Visceral pain is midline because the gut develops as a midline tube.

cards.f: Arteries of the foregut, midgut and hindgut, with levels
cards.b: Coeliac trunk (about T12), superior mesenteric artery (about L1), inferior mesenteric artery (about L3).
cards.ex: Three unpaired anterior branches of the abdominal aorta, in descending order.

cards.f: Why does appendicitis pain move from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa?
cards.b: Early pain is visceral (midgut, referred periumbilically); once the parietal peritoneum is inflamed, its somatic nerves localise pain to the right iliac fossa.
cards.ex: Visceral = vague and midline; parietal = sharp and local.

cards.f: Haematemesis, splenomegaly and caput medusae in a man with cirrhosis: explain the anatomy
cards.b: Portal hypertension opens portosystemic anastomoses: left gastric to oesophageal (varices that bleed) and paraumbilical to abdominal wall veins (caput medusae); splenic congestion enlarges the spleen.
cards.ex: Look for the anastomoses at oesophagus, anorectum, umbilicus and retroperitoneum.

cards.f: What is in Calot's triangle and why does it matter?
cards.b: Bounded by cystic duct, common hepatic duct and inferior liver surface; contains the cystic artery (usually from the right hepatic) and the node of Lund. Defining it before division protects the bile duct and right hepatic artery.
cards.ex: Misidentifying the common bile duct as the cystic duct causes major bile duct injury.

cards.f: Bilirubin and ALP very high, ALT mildly raised, dilated bile ducts on ultrasound
cards.b: Obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice, for example a stone in the common bile duct.
cards.ex: ALP rises most when bile flow is blocked; ALT rises most with hepatocyte injury.

cards.f: Retroperitoneal vs intraperitoneal: duodenum and colon
cards.b: Retroperitoneal: duodenum parts 2–4, ascending and descending colon, pancreas (except tail). Intraperitoneal: first part of the duodenum (mostly), transverse and sigmoid colon (on mesenteries).
cards.ex: Organs on a mesentery are intraperitoneal and mobile.

cards.f: Parts of levator ani
cards.b: Puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus (with coccygeus completing the pelvic diaphragm).
cards.ex: Named by origin and insertion: pubis to rectum, pubis to coccyx, ilium to coccyx.

cards.f: Course of the pudendal nerve
cards.b: S2–S4; leaves through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, crosses the sacrospinous ligament near the ischial spine, re-enters via the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal canal.
cards.ex: Out of the pelvis and back in, hooking around the ischial spine.

cards.f: Landmark for a transvaginal pudendal block
cards.b: The ischial spine, palpated through the lateral vaginal wall; aspirate before injecting because the internal pudendal vessels run with the nerve.
cards.ex: The nerve crosses just behind the ischial spine on the sacrospinous ligament.

cards.f: Anal canal above vs below the pectinate line
cards.b: Above: endoderm, visceral nerves (painless), superior rectal vessels to portal system, internal iliac nodes. Below: ectoderm, somatic nerves (painful), inferior rectal vessels to systemic veins, superficial inguinal nodes.
cards.ex: The line is the old boundary of hindgut and proctodeum.

cards.f: Why are internal haemorrhoids usually painless?
cards.b: They arise above the pectinate line, where the mucosa has visceral (autonomic) supply that senses stretch but not pain.
cards.ex: Pain needs somatic nerves, found only below the line.

cards.f: Why does testicular cancer spread to para-aortic nodes?
cards.b: The testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidneys and keeps its arteries, veins and lymphatics as it descends, so lymph returns to para-aortic nodes.
cards.ex: Scrotal skin, by contrast, drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

cards.f: Autonomic control of bladder filling vs emptying
cards.b: Filling: sympathetic (about T11–L2) relaxes detrusor and closes bladder neck; pudendal keeps external sphincter closed. Emptying: parasympathetic pelvic splanchnics (S2–S4) contract detrusor.
cards.ex: 'Parasympathetic pees.'

cards.f: Why is the ureter at risk during hysterectomy?
cards.b: It passes beneath the uterine artery about 1–2 cm lateral to the cervix, so it can be clamped or tied with the artery.
cards.ex: 'Water under the bridge': ureter (water) under uterine artery (bridge).

cards.f: Painful bright-red bleeding with a split in the posterior anal margin
cards.b: An anal fissure below the pectinate line; somatic inferior rectal nerves make it very painful.
cards.ex: Below the line = somatic = painful.

cards.f: Where would a squamous carcinoma of the lower anal canal first spread?
cards.b: To the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, because tissue below the pectinate line drains there.
cards.ex: Lymph follows the embryological origin of each part of the canal.

cards.f: Branches of the posterior cord
cards.b: Upper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves.
cards.ex: ULTRA: Upper subscapular, Lower subscapular, Thoracodorsal, Radial, Axillary.

cards.f: Why does the arm adopt a 'waiter's tip' posture in Erb palsy?
cards.b: C5–C6 loss paralyses deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps and brachialis; unopposed medial rotators and pronators leave the arm adducted, medially rotated, elbow extended and forearm pronated.
cards.ex: Think of what C5–C6 normally does: abduct, laterally rotate, flex the elbow, supinate.

cards.f: Why can a lower brachial plexus injury cause Horner's syndrome?
cards.b: Preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head leave the cord at T1; avulsion of the T1 root interrupts them, giving ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.
cards.ex: T1 carries the start of the cervical sympathetic outflow.

cards.f: Why is triceps usually spared in a midshaft humeral fracture with radial nerve palsy?
cards.b: The branches to the long and lateral heads of triceps leave the radial nerve above the radial groove, so extension is at most weakened.
cards.ex: The injury level is below those branches.

cards.f: Why is thenar sensation preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome?
cards.b: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises before the wrist and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, outside the tunnel.
cards.ex: Only structures deep to the retinaculum are compressed.

cards.f: What is the ulnar paradox?
cards.b: A wrist ulnar lesion claws the ring and little fingers more than an elbow lesion, because with a wrist lesion the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus still flexes the fingers.
cards.ex: Distal lesion, more clawing; proximal lesion, less.

cards.f: Weak elbow extension, reduced triceps jerk and numb middle finger
cards.b: C7 radiculopathy (e.g. C6/C7 disc prolapse).
cards.ex: Triceps reflex is C7 and the middle finger is the C7 dermatome.

cards.f: Radial nerve palsy vs C7 radiculopathy
cards.b: Radial palsy: wrist drop, triceps and reflex usually preserved, dorsal first web space numb. C7 root: weak triceps, wrist and finger extension and reduced triceps reflex, middle-finger numbness.
cards.ex: The triceps reflex separates them.

cards.f: Scapula wings when pushing against a wall after mastectomy with axillary clearance: which nerve?
cards.b: Long thoracic nerve (C5–C7), supplying serratus anterior.
cards.ex: Serratus anterior holds the scapula against the chest wall.

cards.f: Contents of the carpal tunnel
cards.b: Median nerve and nine tendons: four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus.
cards.ex: Flexor carpi radialis lies in the retinaculum, not the tunnel.

cards.f: Contents of the femoral triangle, lateral to medial
cards.b: Femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, femoral canal (lymphatics). Artery, vein and canal lie in the femoral sheath; the nerve lies outside.
cards.ex: NAVEL: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics.

cards.f: Mid-inguinal point vs midpoint of the inguinal ligament
cards.b: Mid-inguinal point: halfway between ASIS and pubic symphysis, femoral pulse. Midpoint of the inguinal ligament: halfway between ASIS and pubic tubercle, deep inguinal ring.
cards.ex: Symphysis for the pulse; tubercle for the ring.

cards.f: Explain a positive Trendelenburg sign
cards.b: Standing on the affected leg, weak hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus, superior gluteal nerve) cannot hold the pelvis level, so it drops on the opposite side.
cards.ex: The stance-side abductors hold up the other side of the pelvis.

cards.f: Why do displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures risk avascular necrosis?
cards.b: The head is supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running up the neck under the capsule; displacement tears them.
cards.ex: Extracapsular fractures leave these vessels intact.

cards.f: Why is the leg shortened and externally rotated after a displaced neck of femur fracture?
cards.b: Muscles crossing the hip pull the shaft upwards (shortening) and iliopsoas and the short lateral rotators turn it outwards once the neck no longer holds it.
cards.ex: Classic sign of a displaced proximal femoral fracture.

cards.f: Common fibular nerve palsy vs L5 radiculopathy
cards.b: Both give foot drop. L5: inversion (tibial nerve) and hip abduction (superior gluteal nerve) also weak, often with back pain. Fibular palsy: inversion and hip abduction spared; numb lateral leg and dorsum of foot.
cards.ex: Test inversion: it separates them.

cards.f: Why are gluteal intramuscular injections given in the upper outer quadrant?
cards.b: The sciatic nerve passes through the lower medial part of the buttock after leaving below piriformis; the upper outer quadrant (or ventrogluteal site) avoids it.
cards.ex: Injection into the lower medial buttock risks sciatic nerve injury.

cards.f: Knee jerk and ankle jerk roots
cards.b: Knee jerk: L3–L4 (femoral nerve). Ankle jerk: S1 (tibial nerve).
cards.ex: '1, 2 buckle my shoe (S1–S2), 3, 4 kick the door (L3–L4).'

cards.f: Positive Lachman test after a twisting injury with immediate swelling
cards.b: Anterior cruciate ligament tear: the tibia translates forwards on the femur.
cards.ex: ACL resists anterior tibial translation.

cards.f: A displaced intracapsular hip fracture in a frail 84-year-old: fixation or replacement?
cards.b: Replacement arthroplasty (NICE CG124), because the head's blood supply is likely disrupted; total hip replacement is considered for selected, more independent people.
cards.ex: Extracapsular fractures are fixed; displaced intracapsular ones are usually replaced.

cards.f: Contents of the jugular foramen
cards.b: Glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X) and accessory (XI) nerves, the internal jugular vein (from the sigmoid sinus) and the inferior petrosal sinus.
cards.ex: Three nerves plus the main venous outflow of the skull.

cards.f: Foramina for V1, V2 and V3
cards.b: V1: superior orbital fissure. V2: foramen rotundum. V3: foramen ovale.
cards.ex: 'Standing Room Only': Superior orbital fissure, Rotundum, Ovale.

cards.f: Why is a blow to the pterion dangerous?
cards.b: The bone is thin where four bones meet, and it overlies a branch of the middle meningeal artery; a fracture can tear the artery, causing an extradural haematoma.
cards.ex: Arterial bleeding between skull and dura expands quickly.

cards.f: Extradural vs subdural haematoma
cards.b: Extradural: middle meningeal artery, between skull and dura, biconvex, rarely crosses sutures. Subdural: bridging veins, between dura and arachnoid, crescentic, can cross sutures, often older or anticoagulated patients.
cards.ex: Dura is fixed at sutures, which limits extradural spread.

cards.f: Why does an upper motor neuron facial palsy spare the forehead?
cards.b: The facial motor neurons for the upper face receive input from both cerebral hemispheres, so one-sided cortical damage leaves forehead movement largely intact.
cards.ex: Bilateral cortical supply protects the upper face.

cards.f: Whole right face weak, hyperacusis, altered taste, dry right eye
cards.b: Right lower motor neuron facial nerve lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion (greater petrosal, stapedius and chorda tympani involved).
cards.ex: Each branch lost places the lesion higher in the canal.

cards.f: Nerve supply of the tongue
cards.b: Anterior two-thirds: touch via lingual (V3), taste via chorda tympani (VII). Posterior third: IX for both. Muscles: XII, except palatoglossus (X).
cards.ex: Sensation and taste follow the tongue's pharyngeal arch origins.

cards.f: Tongue deviates to the left with left-sided wasting and fasciculation
cards.b: Left hypoglossal (lower motor neuron) lesion: the intact right genioglossus pushes the tongue towards the weak left side.
cards.ex: Lower motor neuron signs (wasting, fasciculation) are on the same side as the lesion.

cards.f: Recurrent vs external laryngeal nerve injury after thyroidectomy
cards.b: Recurrent: vocal fold weakness, hoarseness (unilateral) or stridor and airway compromise (bilateral). External: cricothyroid weakness, loss of high pitch and voice fatigue.
cards.ex: External laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery.

cards.f: Why is the accessory nerve at risk during posterior triangle node biopsy?
cards.b: It crosses the posterior triangle superficially, just under the investing fascia; injury weakens trapezius, causing shoulder droop and difficulty abducting above 90°.
cards.ex: Superficial course = easy to cut.

cards.f: Week 2: the 'week of twos'
cards.b: Bilaminar disc (epiblast, hypoblast); two cavities (amniotic cavity, yolk sac); two trophoblast layers (cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast).
cards.ex: Gastrulation (three layers) follows in week 3.

cards.f: Ectoderm vs mesoderm vs endoderm derivatives
cards.b: Ectoderm: epidermis, nervous system, neural crest. Mesoderm: muscle, bone, heart, vessels, kidneys, gonads. Endoderm: gut and airway lining, liver, pancreas, thyroid follicles.
cards.ex: Outer covering, middle supports, inner linings.

cards.f: Why does failure of the caudal neuropore cause spina bifida?
cards.b: The caudal neuropore normally closes around day 28; if it does not, the lower neural tube and overlying vertebral arches fail to form normally, leaving meninges or cord exposed.
cards.ex: Cranial failure gives anencephaly; caudal failure gives spina bifida.

cards.f: Why does the foramen ovale close at birth?
cards.b: Lung expansion lowers pulmonary resistance, so pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure above right; the flap is pressed against the septum.
cards.ex: Pressure reversal, then later anatomical fusion.

cards.f: Adult remnants of the fetal shunts
cards.b: Ductus arteriosus: ligamentum arteriosum. Ductus venosus: ligamentum venosum. Foramen ovale: fossa ovalis. Umbilical vein: ligamentum teres.
cards.ex: Each shunt leaves a fibrous remnant.

cards.f: Why does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loop lower than the right?
cards.b: It hooks under the sixth arch derivative (ductus arteriosus, now ligamentum arteriosum) beside the aortic arch. On the right the distal sixth arch artery disappears, so the nerve hooks under the subclavian artery (fourth arch).
cards.ex: The nerve is caught by whichever arch artery persists.

cards.f: Third vs fourth pharyngeal pouch derivatives
cards.b: Third: inferior parathyroids and thymus. Fourth: superior parathyroids (and ultimopharyngeal body giving C cells).
cards.ex: The third-pouch glands migrate further, ending up lower.

cards.f: Omphalocele vs gastroschisis
cards.b: Omphalocele: midline at the umbilicus, covered by a membrane, often with other anomalies. Gastroschisis: beside the umbilicus, no sac, bowel exposed.
cards.ex: Sac = omphalocele.

cards.f: Describe midgut rotation
cards.b: The midgut herniates into the cord at about week 6, rotates 270° anticlockwise (viewed from the front) around the superior mesenteric artery and returns by about week 10.
cards.ex: Malrotation leaves a narrow mesentery prone to volvulus.

cards.f: Midline neck lump that rises on tongue protrusion
cards.b: Thyroglossal cyst: a remnant of the thyroglossal duct along the path of thyroid descent from the foramen caecum.
cards.ex: Attachment to the tongue base explains the movement.

cards.f: When should folic acid be started to reduce neural tube defects (NHS advice)?
cards.b: Before pregnancy, ideally about three months before (or as soon as pregnant), continuing for the first 12 weeks.
cards.ex: The neural tube closes by about day 28, often before pregnancy is known.

questions.q: Which ligament of the vertebral column limits hyperextension?
questions.why: The anterior longitudinal ligament runs down the front of the vertebral bodies and discs. Extension separates the front of the bodies, so this ligament becomes taut and limits hyperextension.
optWhy: Ligamentum flavum joins laminae behind the canal; it is stretched in flexion, not extension.
The posterior longitudinal ligament lies on the back of the bodies inside the canal and limits hyperflexion.
Correct: it lies in front of the bodies, so extension pulls it taut.
The supraspinous ligament joins the tips of the spinous processes and is stretched in flexion.
questions.clue: 'Limits hyperextension' means the ligament must lie on the front of the column.
questions.concept: A ligament resists the movement that separates its two attachments.

followUp.q: A driver's head is thrown sharply backwards in a rear-end collision. Which ligament is most likely to be torn by this hyperextension?
followUp.why: Hyperextension opens the front of the column, so the anterior longitudinal ligament is stretched and may tear. The posterior longitudinal, interspinous and nuchal ligaments lie behind the bodies and are stretched in flexion, not extension.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman has severe pain from the buttock down the back of the leg to the lateral border of the foot after lifting. Plantarflexion is weak, the ankle jerk is absent on that side and the knee jerk is normal. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
questions.why: Weak plantarflexion, an absent ankle jerk and sensory change along the lateral foot form the S1 pattern. The usual cause is a posterolateral L5/S1 prolapse compressing the traversing S1 root.
optWhy: Correct: plantarflexion weakness, absent ankle jerk and lateral foot symptoms are the S1 pattern.
L4 causes weak knee extension, a reduced knee jerk and medial leg numbness.
L5 causes weak big-toe extension and ankle dorsiflexion and numbness over the dorsum of the foot; the ankle jerk is usually preserved.
L3 would affect the anterior thigh and the knee jerk, which is normal here.
S2 contributes to plantarflexion but is not the main ankle-jerk root, and isolated S2 lesions give posterior thigh and perineal sensory change rather than this picture.
questions.clue: Absent ankle jerk with lateral foot pain and weak plantarflexion.
questions.concept: Root level from myotome, reflex and dermatome together.

followUp.q: A man has pain down the side of the leg into the top of the foot after an L4/L5 disc prolapse. Big-toe extension is weak and both reflexes are normal. Which root is compressed?
followUp.why: A posterolateral L4/L5 prolapse usually catches the traversing L5 root: weak big-toe extension (extensor hallucis longus), dorsal foot numbness and normal reflexes fit L5. L4 has already exited above the disc and would reduce the knee jerk; S1 would reduce the ankle jerk; L3 affects the anterior thigh.

questions.q: A junior doctor is about to perform a lumbar puncture on an adult. At which interspace is the needle least likely to injure the spinal cord while still reaching CSF?
questions.why: The adult cord usually ends at about L1/L2, and the dural sac with its CSF continues to about S2. L3/L4 lies safely below the cord but within the lumbar cistern.
optWhy: T11/T12 lies over the lower cord; the needle could injure it.
T12/L1 lies over the conus medullaris in most adults.
L1/L2 is where the cord often ends, so it is not safely below it.
Correct: below the conus and within the lumbar cistern.
S2/S3 is at or below the end of the dural sac and the sacrum is fused, so CSF is unlikely to be reached.
questions.clue: 'Least likely to injure the spinal cord while still reaching CSF'.
questions.concept: The cord ends higher than the dural sac, leaving a CSF-filled cistern between them.

followUp.q: During a midline lumbar puncture the needle passes through the ligamentum flavum. Which is the last layer it pierces before CSF can be aspirated?
followUp.why: After the ligamentum flavum come the epidural space, the dura and then the closely applied arachnoid; CSF lies in the subarachnoid space just deep to the arachnoid. The pia covers the cord and roots and is not pierced; the dura is crossed just before the arachnoid.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with three days of sciatica has new difficulty starting to pass urine and numbness around the anus. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure him and review in six weeks
Emergency referral to hospital for MRI
Plain lumbar spine X-ray at the practice
Bladder scan to decide whether imaging is needed
questions.why: Urinary hesitancy and saddle numbness with recent-onset sciatica are red flags for cauda equina syndrome. The England pathway asks for emergency referral and MRI as soon as possible (within four hours of the request).
optWhy: Waiting risks permanent loss of bladder, bowel and sexual function.
Correct: these are red flags needing emergency MRI.
Physiotherapy suits uncomplicated sciatica, not suspected cauda equina compression.
X-ray does not show discs or roots, and it would delay the right test.
The pathway warns that a bladder scan must not be used alone to decide on MRI.
questions.clue: New urinary hesitancy plus perianal numbness.
questions.concept: Sacral root compression (cauda equina syndrome) is a surgical emergency diagnosed by MRI.

followUp.q: Which dermatomes supply the 'saddle' area tested when cauda equina syndrome is suspected?
followUp.why: The perianal, perineal and genital skin is supplied by S2–S5, the lowest roots of the cauda equina. L1–L2 supply the groin and upper thigh, L4–L5 the leg and foot, and T10–T12 the abdominal wall.

questions.q: Explain why lumbar puncture is performed at the L3/L4 or L4/L5 interspace, name the surface landmark used to find this level, and list the layers the needle crosses in the midline.
markScheme: The adult spinal cord ends (conus medullaris) at about L1/L2
The dural sac and subarachnoid space continue to about S2, forming the lumbar cistern containing CSF and cauda equina roots
At L3/L4 or L4/L5 the needle is below the cord; roots float and move aside
Landmark: the line joining the highest points of the iliac crests (supracristal or Tuffier's line) at about L4 or L4/L5; it is approximate
Layers: skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura and arachnoid, then subarachnoid space
questions.modelAnswer: In adults the spinal cord tapers into the conus medullaris at about the L1/L2 level, but the dural sac continues to about S2. Between them lies the lumbar cistern, a widened part of the subarachnoid space containing CSF and the nerve roots of the cauda equina. A needle placed at L3/L4 or L4/L5 is therefore below the cord, and the roots, floating in CSF, tend to move aside. The level is found using the line joining the highest points of the iliac crests (the supracristal or Tuffier's line), which crosses roughly the L4 spinous process or the L4/L5 interspace; this landmark is imprecise, so the interspace is chosen at or below it. In the midline the needle passes through skin and subcutaneous tissue, the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, the ligamentum flavum (felt as a give), the epidural space, the dura and arachnoid, and then enters the subarachnoid space, where CSF can be collected.
questions.concept: The cord ends higher than the dural sac, creating a safe CSF-filled lumbar cistern.

questions.q:
A 42-year-old warehouse worker felt sudden low back pain while lifting a heavy box. Over the next day the pain spread down the back of his left thigh into the outer side of his foot. Straight-leg raising on the left produces leg pain at 35°. Plantarflexion of the left foot is weak and he cannot stand on tiptoe on that side. The left ankle jerk is absent, the knee jerks are normal, and pinprick is reduced over the lateral border of the left foot. Perianal sensation and bladder function are normal.

Identify the most likely level and nerve root involved, explain the anatomy that produces each finding, and outline the red-flag features that would change the urgency of management.
markScheme: Most likely posterolateral L5/S1 disc prolapse compressing the left S1 root
Posterolateral prolapse catches the traversing root (S1 at L5/S1) because L5 has already exited above the disc
Disc anatomy: annulus weakest posterolaterally where the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow
Weak plantarflexion: gastrocnemius and soleus, mainly S1–S2 via the tibial nerve; absent ankle jerk = S1 reflex arc; normal knee jerk shows L3–L4 intact
Lateral foot sensory loss matches the S1 dermatome; positive straight-leg raise reflects tension on an irritated root through the sciatic nerve

Red flags of cauda equina syndrome: urinary hesitancy or altered sensation of flow, saddle (S2–S5) numbness, loss of rectal fullness sensation, severe or progressive bilateral leg weakness, new sexual dysfunction
These need emergency referral and MRI as soon as possible (England pathway: within four hours of request); bladder scan should not decide alone
Other features prompting urgent assessment: progressive weakness, fever, weight loss, history of cancer, significant trauma
questions.modelAnswer:
The picture fits a posterolateral prolapse of the L5/S1 disc compressing the left S1 nerve root. The annulus fibrosus is weakest posterolaterally, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow, so the nucleus pulposus tends to herniate there. At L5/S1 the L5 root has already left through the upper part of its foramen above the disc, so a posterolateral bulge catches the traversing S1 root as it heads for the S1 foramen.

Each finding maps onto S1:
- Pain down the back of the thigh to the outer foot follows the course of the sciatic nerve and the S1 dermatome.
- Weak plantarflexion and inability to stand on tiptoe reflect gastrocnemius and soleus, supplied mainly by S1–S2 through the tibial nerve.
- The absent ankle jerk shows interruption of the S1 reflex arc, while the normal knee jerk shows that L3–L4 are intact.
- Reduced sensation on the lateral border of the foot matches the S1 dermatome. An L5 lesion would instead affect the dorsum of the foot and big toe and weaken big-toe extension.
- A positive straight-leg raise at a low angle means that stretching the sciatic nerve pulls on an irritated, tethered root.

Red flags change the urgency. Cauda equina syndrome is suggested by difficulty starting to pass urine or reduced sensation of urine flow, altered perianal, perineal or genital sensation (the S2–S5 dermatomes), loss of the sensation of rectal fullness, severe or progressive weakness in both legs, or new sexual dysfunction. The national pathway for England asks for emergency referral and MRI as soon as possible, within four hours of the request, and warns against relying on a bladder scan alone. Progressive weakness also needs urgent imaging, and fever, weight loss, a history of cancer, immunosuppression or significant trauma raise the possibility of infection, malignancy or fracture. Without red flags, most disc prolapses settle with conservative care, and imaging is reserved for persistent or worsening symptoms.
questions.concept: Root localisation from myotome, reflex and dermatome; cauda equina red flags.

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the oesophagus pass through the diaphragm?
questions.why: The oesophageal hiatus lies at T10 and transmits the oesophagus with the vagal trunks. The IVC passes at T8 and the aorta at T12.
optWhy: T8 is the caval opening for the IVC.
T12 is the aortic hiatus.
Correct: the oesophagus and vagal trunks pass at T10.
L1 is the transpyloric plane; no main diaphragmatic opening lies there.
questions.clue: 'Oesophagus' and 'diaphragm'.
questions.concept: Levels of the three main diaphragmatic openings.

followUp.q: Which structure passes through the diaphragm at T8 together with the IVC?
options: Branches of the right phrenic nerve
followUp.why: Terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve accompany the IVC through the caval opening at T8. The vagal trunks pass with the oesophagus at T10; the thoracic duct and azygos vein pass with the aorta at T12.

questions.q: A chest drain is to be inserted for a large pneumothorax. Why is the needle and then the tube passed immediately above the upper border of a rib?
options: To stay away from the internal thoracic artery
Because the pleura is thinnest there
To avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle in the costal groove of the rib above
To avoid the long thoracic nerve
Because the intercostal muscles are absent there
questions.why: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Passing just above the rib below keeps instruments away from the main bundle.
optWhy: The internal thoracic artery runs beside the sternum and is avoided by staying lateral, not by choice of rib border.
Pleural thickness does not vary in this way.
Correct: the bundle lies under the rib above, so the upper border of the rib below is safer.
The long thoracic nerve is avoided by staying in front of the mid-axillary line, not by the rib border.
All three intercostal muscle layers are present across the space.
questions.clue: 'Immediately above the upper border of a rib'.
questions.concept: Position of the intercostal neurovascular bundle.

followUp.q: A doctor inserting a pleural aspiration needle strikes the lower border of a rib and draws back bright red blood. Which vessel has most likely been injured?
options: Posterior intercostal artery in the costal groove
followUp.why: The intercostal artery runs in the costal groove on the lower border of the rib, so a needle passed along that border can puncture it. The internal thoracic artery is parasternal, the subclavian lies above the first rib and the pulmonary artery is in the lung root.

questions.q: A 23-year-old with a stab wound to the left chest has a respiratory rate of 34/min, blood pressure 80/50 mmHg, a trachea deviated to the right, a hyperresonant left chest with absent breath sounds and distended neck veins. What best explains his hypotension?
options: Impaired venous return from raised intrathoracic pressure and mediastinal shift
Blood loss into the left pleural space
Cardiac tamponade from a right ventricular wound
questions.why: This is a tension pneumothorax: hyperresonance with absent breath sounds shows air, and tracheal deviation shows mediastinal shift. Raised pressure kinks and compresses the great veins, so venous return and cardiac output fall while the neck veins fill.
optWhy: Correct: air under tension impairs venous return.
A haemothorax would be dull to percussion, and blood loss would give flat neck veins.
Tamponade raises the JVP but does not cause a hyperresonant hemithorax or tracheal deviation.
A vasovagal reaction would not explain the chest signs or raised JVP.
Hypoxia contributes to distress but does not explain the raised JVP with mediastinal shift.
questions.clue: Hyperresonant chest, deviated trachea and distended neck veins together.
questions.concept: Tension pneumothorax impairs venous return.

followUp.q: After a stab wound, a patient's left chest is dull to percussion with absent breath sounds, the trachea is central and the neck veins are flat. Blood pressure is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
followUp.why: Dullness indicates fluid, and flat neck veins with hypotension indicate blood loss: a haemothorax. Tension pneumothorax is hyperresonant with distended veins; tamponade gives distended veins and muffled heart sounds with clear lung fields; a simple pneumothorax is hyperresonant.

questions.q: A 66-year-old has chest pain with ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF and a heart rate of 44/min. Angiography shows a right-dominant circulation. Occlusion of which artery best explains both the ECG and the slow heart rate?
questions.why: Leads II, III and aVF view the inferior wall, which in a right-dominant heart is supplied by the posterior interventricular branch of the RCA. The RCA also usually supplies the SA node and, in right dominance, the AV node, so bradycardia and heart block are common.
optWhy: The LAD supplies the anterior wall and anterior septum (V1–V4), not the inferior wall.
The circumflex supplies the lateral wall; it gives the inferior supply only in left-dominant hearts.
Left main occlusion causes extensive anterior and lateral ischaemia and usually shock.
Correct: inferior territory plus nodal supply in a right-dominant heart.
Diagonal branches supply the anterolateral wall (I, aVL).
questions.clue: Inferior leads, bradycardia and right dominance.
questions.concept: Coronary territories and nodal supply.

followUp.q: A patient has ST elevation in leads V1–V4. Which artery is most likely occluded?
followUp.why: V1–V4 face the septum and anterior left ventricle, supplied by the LAD. The RCA and posterior interventricular artery supply the inferior wall in most people; the circumflex supplies the lateral wall.

questions.q: Explain why a lesion of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve can be the first sign of a thoracic tumour, whereas a right-sided lesion is unlikely to be.
markScheme: Both recurrent laryngeal nerves branch from the vagus and supply all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid
The left nerve hooks under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum in the thorax, then climbs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove
The right nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery in the root of the neck and never enters the thorax
So lung apex or mediastinal tumours, nodes or an aortic aneurysm can stretch or invade the left nerve, causing hoarseness
questions.modelAnswer: Each recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus that supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid, so injury weakens one vocal fold and causes hoarseness. The two nerves have different courses because of how the arch arteries develop. The left nerve leaves the vagus in the thorax, hooks under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum and then climbs back to the larynx in the tracheo-oesophageal groove. The right nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery at the root of the neck and does not enter the thorax. A tumour of the left lung or mediastinum, enlarged mediastinal nodes or an aneurysm of the aortic arch can therefore stretch or invade the left nerve and present first with hoarseness, whereas thoracic disease rarely reaches the right nerve.
questions.concept: The asymmetric course of the recurrent laryngeal nerves follows the arch arteries.

questions.q:
A 23-year-old man is stabbed in the left side of the chest. He arrives breathless, with a respiratory rate of 32/min, oxygen saturation of 88% on air and a heart rate of 128/min. The trachea is deviated to the right, the left hemithorax is hyperresonant with absent breath sounds, and his neck veins are distended. His blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg. A wound is seen in the left fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line.

Explain the anatomy behind his signs. Describe where you would decompress the chest and then insert a chest drain, naming the layers traversed and the structures at risk, and explain why the drain is passed over the upper border of the rib.
markScheme: Tension pneumothorax: wound acts as a one-way valve, air accumulates under pressure in the pleural space
