Lung collapse and mediastinal shift to the right explain tracheal deviation; raised intrathoracic pressure and venous kinking reduce venous return: distended neck veins, hypotension, tachycardia
Hyperresonance and absent breath sounds: air between chest wall and collapsed lung
Clinical diagnosis: decompress before imaging; second intercostal space midclavicular line or the lateral site (fifth space, anterior axillary line), reported to have higher success
Chest drain in the triangle of safety: lateral border of pectoralis major, anterior border of latissimus dorsi, line of the fifth intercostal space, apex below the axilla
Layers: skin, subcutaneous tissue, serratus anterior, external, internal and innermost intercostals, endothoracic fascia, parietal pleura; blunt dissection, no sharp trocar
Neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve) in the costal groove under the rib above, between internal and innermost layers, so pass over the upper border of the rib below
Structures at risk: intercostal vessels and nerve, long thoracic nerve behind, internal thoracic vessels anteriorly, liver or spleen and diaphragm if too low
questions.modelAnswer:
He has a left tension pneumothorax. The stab wound acts as a one-way valve: air enters the pleural space on each breath but cannot leave. Pleural pressure rises above atmospheric, the left lung collapses and the mediastinum is pushed to the right, deviating the trachea. Raised intrathoracic pressure and mediastinal shift compress and kink the great veins, reducing venous return; the neck veins fill while cardiac output falls, giving hypotension and a compensatory tachycardia. Air between the chest wall and the collapsed lung makes the hemithorax hyperresonant with absent breath sounds, and the collapsed lung explains his hypoxaemia. This is a clinical diagnosis and is treated before imaging.

Immediate decompression is by needle (or, in trained hands, finger) thoracostomy. The traditional site is the second intercostal space in the midclavicular line; the fifth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line is reported to have higher success and fewer complications. A chest drain follows.

The drain is placed in the triangle of safety, bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a horizontal line at about the fifth intercostal space, with its apex below the axilla. After local anaesthetic, the operator incises the skin and uses blunt dissection through subcutaneous tissue, serratus anterior and the external, internal and innermost intercostal muscles, then the endothoracic fascia and parietal pleura. A finger sweep confirms entry before the tube is passed; sharp trocars are avoided because they can injure lung, heart or abdominal organs.

The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove under the lower border of each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Passing just over the upper border of the rib below keeps instruments away from the main bundle, which also explains why posterior approaches, where the rib gives less cover, are avoided. Other structures at risk are the long thoracic nerve on serratus anterior behind the triangle (winging of the scapula), the internal thoracic vessels anteriorly, and the diaphragm, spleen or liver if the drain is placed too low. Pain at the site comes from the intercostal nerve and the parietal pleura, which is why both are generously anaesthetised.
questions.concept: Tension pneumothorax physiology and safe pleural access.

questions.q: Which artery supplies the midgut?
questions.why: The superior mesenteric artery, arising at about L1, supplies the midgut from the second part of the duodenum to about two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon.
optWhy: The coeliac trunk supplies the foregut.
The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut.
Correct: the SMA supplies the midgut.
The internal iliac artery supplies pelvic organs and the lower rectum, not the midgut.
questions.clue: 'Midgut'.
questions.concept: One artery per embryological gut region.

followUp.q: Where is the pain of early small-bowel obstruction (a midgut structure) typically felt?
followUp.why: Visceral pain from the midgut, including the small bowel, is referred to the periumbilical region. Foregut pain is epigastric, hindgut pain suprapubic, and shoulder-tip pain comes from diaphragmatic irritation.

questions.q: During an open inguinal hernia repair, the surgeon finds a sac bulging through the posterior wall of the canal medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. What type of hernia is this?
questions.why: A sac emerging medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through the posterior wall lies within Hesselbach's triangle, which defines a direct inguinal hernia.
optWhy: An indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
A femoral hernia passes below the inguinal ligament through the femoral canal.
An obturator hernia passes through the obturator canal in the pelvis.
A Spigelian hernia occurs at the lateral edge of rectus abdominis, above the inguinal canal.
Correct: medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, through the posterior wall.
questions.clue: 'Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels'.
questions.concept: Hernias are classified by their relation to the inferior epigastric vessels.

followUp.q: A 4-month-old boy has an intermittent groin swelling extending into the scrotum. At surgery a sac is found within the spermatic cord, entering the deep ring. Which embryological structure has failed to close?
followUp.why: An indirect inguinal hernia in infancy follows a patent processus vaginalis, the peritoneal outpouching that accompanies testicular descent. The urachus links bladder and umbilicus, the vitelline duct links midgut and yolk sac, and the gubernaculum guides descent but is not a peritoneal channel.

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman has a tender, irreducible lump in the groin that lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Which hernia is most likely, and why is it prone to strangulation?
options: Direct inguinal hernia, because Hesselbach's triangle is wide
Indirect inguinal hernia, because the deep ring is wide
Femoral hernia, because the femoral ring is narrow and unyielding
Umbilical hernia, because of a narrow umbilical ring
Obturator hernia, because it lies deep
questions.why: A lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle has passed through the femoral canal under the inguinal ligament. The femoral ring is bounded by the inguinal and lacunar ligaments and the pectineal ligament, so a hernia here is easily trapped and strangulated.
optWhy: Direct hernias lie above and medial to the pubic tubercle and have wide necks, so they rarely strangulate.
Indirect hernias emerge above and medial to the tubercle at the superficial ring.
Correct: femoral position and a narrow, rigid ring.
An umbilical hernia lies at the umbilicus, not the groin.
Obturator hernias are deep in the thigh and seldom form a visible groin lump.
questions.clue: 'Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle'.
questions.concept: The pubic tubercle separates inguinal from femoral hernias.

followUp.q: Which structure lies immediately lateral to the femoral canal within the femoral sheath?
followUp.why: Within the femoral sheath, from lateral to medial, are the femoral artery, femoral vein and femoral canal, so the vein lies immediately lateral to the canal. The femoral nerve lies outside the sheath, and the great saphenous vein joins the femoral vein from the front.

questions.q: A 19-year-old has 10 hours of dull central abdominal pain that has now moved to the right iliac fossa and is worse on coughing. Which best explains the change in the site of pain?
options: Visceral pain from a midgut organ has been replaced by somatic pain from inflamed parietal peritoneum
The appendix has moved within the abdomen
The inflammation has spread to the hindgut
Referred pain via the phrenic nerve
The pain now arises from the right ureter
questions.why: The appendix is a midgut derivative, so stretch of its wall is felt as poorly localised periumbilical pain. When inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, its somatic supply from the abdominal wall localises the pain to the right iliac fossa, and movement or coughing aggravates it.
optWhy: Correct: visceral then parietal peritoneal pain.
The appendix does not move; the change reflects which nerves carry the pain.
Hindgut pain would be suprapubic, and the appendix is midgut.
Phrenic referral gives shoulder-tip pain, not right iliac fossa pain.
Ureteric pain is colicky loin-to-groin pain, not peritonitic pain worse on coughing.
questions.clue: Central pain moving to the right iliac fossa, worse on coughing.
questions.concept: Visceral versus parietal peritoneal pain.

followUp.q: A patient with cholecystitis first has epigastric pain, then sharp right upper quadrant pain worse on deep breathing. Which nerves carry the later pain?
options: Somatic nerves of the parietal peritoneum under the right costal margin
Sympathetic visceral afferents from the gallbladder
followUp.why: Once the inflamed gallbladder touches the parietal peritoneum, somatic nerves of the abdominal wall (and centrally the phrenic nerve) localise the pain, and breathing moves the inflamed surfaces. Early epigastric pain is visceral via sympathetic afferents of the foregut; the vagus does not carry this pain, and the pudendal nerve supplies the perineum.

questions.q: Explain why the pain of early appendicitis starts around the umbilicus and later moves to the right iliac fossa, and give the surface marking of McBurney's point.
markScheme: Appendix is a midgut derivative supplied by the appendicular branch of the ileocolic artery (from the SMA)
Visceral afferents travel with sympathetic nerves to about T10, so early pain is referred to the periumbilical (T10) region
Visceral pain is dull, poorly localised and stretch-related
Inflammation then irritates parietal peritoneum, which has somatic innervation and localises pain to the right iliac fossa, worse with movement or coughing
McBurney's point: one third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus
questions.modelAnswer: The appendix develops from the midgut and is supplied by the appendicular branch of the ileocolic artery, a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. Its visceral afferent fibres travel with sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at about T10, the segment that also supplies the skin around the umbilicus. Early in appendicitis, distension and inflammation of the appendix wall cause dull, poorly localised pain that is felt periumbilically. As inflammation spreads through the wall it reaches the parietal peritoneum of the right iliac fossa. The parietal peritoneum has somatic innervation from the nerves of the abdominal wall, so the pain becomes sharp and well localised, and is made worse by movement, coughing or pressure. The point of maximal tenderness is classically McBurney's point, one third of the way along a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.
questions.concept: Visceral pain follows embryological segment; parietal pain is somatic and local.

questions.q: Which spinal roots form the pudendal nerve?
questions.why: The pudendal nerve arises from the anterior rami of S2–S4 in the sacral plexus. 'S2, 3, 4 keeps the pelvic floor off the floor' also recalls the pelvic splanchnic nerves.
optWhy: L4–S1 contributes to the lumbosacral trunk and sciatic nerve, not the pudendal nerve.
S1–S3 omits S4 and includes S1, which is not a pudendal root.
Correct: S2–S4.
S3–S5 includes S5, which forms the coccygeal plexus.
questions.clue: 'Pudendal nerve' and 'roots'.
questions.concept: Sacral roots S2–S4 control perineal muscles and continence.

followUp.q: A woman has lost voluntary control of her external anal sphincter after a difficult forceps delivery. Damage to which branch is most likely?
followUp.why: The inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve supplies the external anal sphincter and perianal skin. The dorsal nerve of the clitoris is sensory to the clitoris; the obturator nerve supplies the thigh adductors; the ilioinguinal nerve supplies groin skin.

questions.q: A 52-year-old has painless bright-red bleeding on the toilet paper. Proctoscopy shows swollen vascular cushions above the pectinate line. What best explains why they are painless?
options: They drain to the systemic veins
The mucosa above the pectinate line has visceral innervation
They are supplied by the inferior rectal nerve
They are covered by keratinised skin
They lie outside the external sphincter
questions.why: Above the pectinate line the canal is hindgut-derived and has autonomic (visceral) supply that senses stretch but not pain, so internal haemorrhoids usually bleed painlessly.
optWhy: Above the line the veins drain to the portal system via the superior rectal vein, and venous drainage does not decide pain anyway.
Correct: visceral innervation above the line.
The inferior rectal nerve supplies the canal below the pectinate line.
Above the line the lining is columnar mucosa, not skin.
Internal haemorrhoids lie inside the canal, deep to the external sphincter's skin margin.
questions.clue: 'Above the pectinate line' and 'painless'.
questions.concept: Innervation changes across the pectinate line.

followUp.q: A patient has a tender, bluish lump at the anal margin below the pectinate line that appeared suddenly and is very painful. Why does it hurt?
options: It is supplied by the superior rectal artery
It drains to the portal system
It is supplied by somatic inferior rectal nerves
It is lined by columnar epithelium
followUp.why: A thrombosed external haemorrhoid lies below the pectinate line, where somatic inferior rectal (pudendal) nerves carry pain. Portal drainage, the superior rectal artery and columnar epithelium all belong to the part of the canal above the line.

questions.q: A 29-year-old man has a painless hard testicular lump confirmed as a germ-cell tumour. Which lymph nodes are the first site of spread?
questions.why: The testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and descends with its vessels and lymphatics, so its lymph returns to the para-aortic nodes around the level of the renal vessels.
optWhy: Superficial inguinal nodes drain scrotal skin, not the testis.
Deep inguinal nodes receive lymph from the superficial inguinal nodes and the lower limb.
Axillary nodes drain the upper limb and breast.
Internal iliac nodes drain pelvic organs such as the prostate and lower rectum.
Correct: para-aortic nodes, reflecting the testis's origin.
questions.clue: 'Testicular' tumour, first nodal site.
questions.concept: Lymphatic drainage follows embryological origin.

followUp.q: A man has a squamous cell carcinoma of the skin of the scrotum. Which nodes are most likely involved first?
followUp.why: Scrotal skin, like other skin of the perineum below the umbilicus, drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. The testis drains to the para-aortic nodes; internal iliac nodes drain pelvic viscera; coeliac nodes drain the foregut.

questions.q: After a total abdominal hysterectomy, a 46-year-old woman develops left loin pain and a rising creatinine. Where was the structure most likely injured?
options: Where the round ligament enters the deep inguinal ring
Where the ovarian vessels cross the pelvic brim
Where the ureter passes beneath the uterine artery beside the cervix
Where the internal iliac artery divides
At the ureteric orifice inside the bladder
questions.why: The ureter runs beneath the uterine artery about 1–2 cm lateral to the cervix, so it can be clamped or tied when the artery is secured. A tied ureter obstructs the kidney, causing loin pain and a rising creatinine.
optWhy: The round ligament passes to the deep inguinal ring, well away from the ureter.
The ureter crosses the pelvic brim near the ovarian vessels and is at some risk there when the infundibulopelvic ligament is tied, but the cervical relation is the classic hysterectomy site.
Correct: 'water under the bridge' beside the cervix is the classic site.
The ureter crosses near the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, but this is not usually disturbed in hysterectomy.
The ureteric orifice is inside the bladder and not part of a standard hysterectomy dissection.
questions.clue: Hysterectomy followed by loin pain and rising creatinine.
questions.concept: Relation of the ureter to the uterine artery.

followUp.q: In the male pelvis, which structure crosses above the ureter as it approaches the bladder?
followUp.why: The ductus deferens crosses above (superficial to) the ureter near the bladder, the male equivalent of the uterine artery's relation in the female. The internal pudendal artery leaves the pelvis; the obturator nerve runs on the side wall; the seminal vesicle lies behind the bladder below the ureter's entry.

questions.q: Describe the lymphatic drainage of the testis and of the scrotal skin, and explain the clinical significance.
markScheme: Testis drains along the testicular vessels to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes near the renal vessels
Reason: the testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and descends with its vessels and lymphatics
Scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes
Significance: testicular cancer is staged by imaging the para-aortic nodes, while inguinal nodes suggest scrotal skin involvement
questions.modelAnswer: The testis develops high on the posterior abdominal wall and descends through the inguinal canal into the scrotum, taking its arteries, veins and lymphatics with it. Its lymph therefore travels back along the testicular vessels in the spermatic cord to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes around the level of the renal vessels. The skin of the scrotum is part of the perineal skin and drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. The clinical consequence is that a testicular tumour spreads first to para-aortic nodes, so these are assessed on CT when staging, and a hard testicular lump is examined without expecting groin node enlargement. Enlarged inguinal nodes in a man with a scrotal problem point instead to disease of the scrotal skin.
questions.concept: Lymphatic drainage follows embryological origin.

questions.q: Which cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to the ulnar nerve?
questions.why: The ulnar nerve (C8–T1) is the main continuation of the medial cord, which also contributes the medial root of the median nerve.
optWhy: The lateral cord gives the musculocutaneous nerve and lateral root of the median nerve.
The posterior cord gives the axillary and radial nerves.
Correct: the ulnar nerve comes from the medial cord.
The upper trunk gives the suprascapular nerve.
questions.clue: 'Ulnar nerve'.
questions.concept: Branches of the brachial plexus cords.

followUp.q: A stab wound in the axilla damages the posterior cord. Which pair of functions is most likely lost?
options: Shoulder abduction beyond 15° and wrist extension
followUp.why: The posterior cord gives the axillary nerve (deltoid: abduction beyond the first 15°) and the radial nerve (wrist and finger extension). Elbow flexion and supination are musculocutaneous (lateral cord); finger abduction and thumb adduction are ulnar (medial cord); opposition is median.

questions.q: A 34-year-old falls and fractures the shaft of her humerus. She cannot extend her wrist or fingers and has numbness over the back of the hand near the base of the thumb. Elbow extension is present but slightly weak. Which nerve has been injured, and where?
options: Axillary nerve at the surgical neck
Ulnar nerve at the medial epicondyle
Radial nerve in the radial groove
Posterior interosseous nerve in the forearm
questions.why: Wrist and finger drop with numbness over the dorsal first web space is the radial nerve. A midshaft fracture injures it in the radial groove, below the branches to the long and lateral heads of triceps, so elbow extension is only weakened.
optWhy: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and the regimental-badge area, not wrist extensors.
The ulnar nerve supplies intrinsic hand muscles and the medial one and a half digits.
The median nerve flexes the wrist and fingers and supplies the palmar lateral digits.
Correct: radial nerve in the radial groove.
The posterior interosseous nerve causes finger drop without sensory loss, because it is purely motor.
questions.clue: Midshaft humerus, wrist drop, dorsal web-space numbness, triceps partly preserved.
questions.concept: Level of radial nerve injury from what is spared.

followUp.q: A man wakes after falling asleep with his arm over a chair back and has wrist drop. Sensation over the dorsal first web space is reduced and his triceps reflex is normal. Where is the lesion most likely?
options: Radial nerve in the spiral (radial) groove
followUp.why: Compression of the radial nerve against the humerus ('Saturday night palsy') gives wrist drop and dorsal web-space numbness with triceps and its reflex preserved. A C7 root lesion reduces the triceps reflex; a posterior cord lesion also weakens deltoid; a posterior interosseous lesion spares sensation.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman wakes at night with tingling in her thumb, index and middle fingers, relieved by shaking her hand. Sensation over the thenar eminence is normal, and there is mild wasting of abductor pollicis brevis. Which is the best explanation for the normal thenar sensation?
options: The thenar skin is supplied by the radial nerve
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
The recurrent motor branch carries thenar sensation
The ulnar nerve supplies the thenar skin
questions.why: This is carpal tunnel syndrome. The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves above the wrist and runs superficial to the flexor retinaculum, so it escapes compression and thenar skin sensation is preserved.
optWhy: The radial nerve supplies the dorsum near the thumb, not the thenar palm.
Correct: the branch bypasses the tunnel.
The recurrent branch is motor to the thenar muscles; it carries no skin sensation.
The ulnar nerve supplies the medial palm and medial one and a half digits.
Both motor and sensory fibres in the tunnel are compressed; the patient's finger tingling shows sensory involvement.
questions.clue: Digit tingling at night but normal thenar sensation.
questions.concept: Course of the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve.

followUp.q: A carpenter cuts the front of his wrist and the median nerve is divided just proximal to the flexor retinaculum, after the palmar cutaneous branch has left. Which deficit is expected?
options: Loss of thenar skin sensation only
Weak thumb opposition with numb palmar lateral three and a half digits
followUp.why: Division at the wrist after the palmar cutaneous branch has left removes the recurrent motor branch (opposition and abduction of the thumb) and digital sensation, but spares thenar skin. Wrist drop is radial and finger abduction is ulnar.

questions.q: A 40-year-old has clawing of the ring and little fingers, wasting of the interossei and a positive Froment's sign after a deep laceration at the front of the wrist. Why is the clawing more marked than it would be after an elbow lesion?
options: The lumbricals are spared in a wrist lesion
The radial nerve is also injured
The median nerve takes over interossei function
The ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus still works and flexes the fingers
questions.why: In the ulnar paradox, a wrist lesion spares the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus (supplied in the forearm), which pulls the distal interphalangeal joints into flexion. Combined with loss of the medial lumbricals this exaggerates the claw. An elbow lesion also paralyses this part of FDP, so the claw is less obvious.
optWhy: The medial two lumbricals are ulnar-supplied and paralysed in both wrist and elbow lesions.
Nothing suggests radial involvement, and it would not increase clawing.
The median nerve does not supply the interossei.
Flexor carpi ulnaris is supplied in the forearm and is spared by a wrist lesion; its loss would not explain more clawing.
Correct: preserved FDP accentuates the claw.
questions.clue: Wrist laceration, marked clawing.
questions.concept: The ulnar paradox.

followUp.q: A man has numbness of the little finger and weakness of finger abduction. Sensation over the dorsal medial hand is also lost. Where is the ulnar nerve lesion most likely?
options: In Guyon's canal at the wrist
In the palm distal to the hook of hamate
followUp.why: The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve leaves in the forearm, so loss of dorsal medial hand sensation places the lesion above that point, most commonly at the elbow (cubital tunnel). A lesion in Guyon's canal or the palm spares the dorsal branch; C5 does not supply the hand.

questions.q: Explain the 'ulnar paradox' and use it to predict the hand posture after an ulnar nerve lesion at the elbow compared with one at the wrist.
markScheme: Ulnar nerve supplies flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus in the forearm, and most intrinsic hand muscles including the medial two lumbricals and interossei
Loss of lumbricals and interossei: MCP joints extend and IP joints flex (claw) in ring and little fingers
Wrist lesion: FDP to ring and little fingers is intact, so DIP flexion is strong and the claw is marked
Elbow lesion: FDP to ring and little fingers is also paralysed, so IP flexion is weaker and the claw less obvious
Paradox: the more proximal lesion produces the less obvious deformity; both show interosseous wasting and positive Froment's sign
questions.modelAnswer: The ulnar nerve supplies flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus in the forearm, then most of the intrinsic muscles of the hand, including the interossei and the medial two lumbricals. Normally the lumbricals and interossei flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints. When they are paralysed, the long extensors hyperextend the MCP joints and the long flexors flex the IP joints of the ring and little fingers, producing a claw. After a wrist lesion, flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers is still working, so the distal interphalangeal joints are pulled strongly into flexion and the claw is marked. After an elbow lesion, that part of profundus is paralysed too, so IP flexion is weaker and the claw is less obvious, even though the injury is more extensive. This is the paradox: the more proximal lesion gives the milder deformity. Both lesions show interosseous wasting, weak finger abduction and adduction and a positive Froment's sign.
questions.concept: The ulnar paradox.

questions.q:
A 25-year-old motorcyclist is thrown from his bike and lands on his right shoulder with his head forced sharply to the left. He is brought in with his right arm hanging by his side, medially rotated, with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated. He cannot abduct the shoulder or flex the elbow. Sensation is reduced over the lateral arm and forearm. Hand movements are normal.

Explain the injury and the posture using the anatomy of the brachial plexus. Describe how the picture would differ after a lower plexus injury, and outline how examination helps distinguish root avulsion from a more distal lesion.
markScheme: Upper trunk (C5–C6) traction injury: Erb palsy, from widening of the neck–shoulder angle
Loss of suprascapular nerve (supraspinatus, infraspinatus) and axillary nerve (deltoid, teres minor): no abduction or lateral rotation
Loss of musculocutaneous nerve (biceps, brachialis) and C5–6 supply to supinator and biceps: no elbow flexion or supination
Unopposed medial rotators and pronators give 'waiter's tip' posture
Sensory loss over C5–C6 dermatomes (lateral arm and forearm); hand normal because C8–T1 intact
Lower plexus (C8–T1, Klumpke): traction on abducted arm; intrinsic hand weakness, clawing, medial forearm and hand numbness; Horner's syndrome if T1 avulsed
Root avulsion suggested by loss of muscles supplied directly from roots (rhomboids via dorsal scapular, serratus anterior via long thoracic: winging), Horner's syndrome, phrenic involvement
Imaging and nerve studies; avulsion has a worse prognosis than more distal stretch injuries
questions.modelAnswer:
The injury forced the head away from the shoulder, widening the angle between them and stretching the upper roots and upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5–C6). This is an Erb palsy.

The upper trunk gives the suprascapular nerve and contributes most fibres to the axillary and musculocutaneous nerves. Loss of supraspinatus (which starts abduction) and deltoid (which continues it) means he cannot abduct the shoulder. Loss of infraspinatus and teres minor removes lateral rotation, so subscapularis, pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi, which receive lower-root fibres, pull the arm into medial rotation. Biceps and brachialis (musculocutaneous) are paralysed, so the elbow cannot flex and hangs extended, and loss of biceps and supinator leaves pronation unopposed. The result is the 'waiter's tip' posture. Sensory loss over the lateral arm and forearm matches the C5–C6 dermatomes, including the regimental-badge area (axillary) and lateral forearm (musculocutaneous). The hand works normally because the C8–T1 roots and the ulnar and median supply to the intrinsic muscles are intact.

A lower plexus (C8–T1) injury, a Klumpke palsy, follows traction on an abducted arm, such as grabbing a branch during a fall. It weakens the intrinsic hand muscles, giving a claw hand, and numbs the medial forearm and hand. If the T1 root is avulsed close to the cord, the preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head are interrupted and Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) appears.

Examination helps decide whether roots have been torn from the cord (pre-ganglionic avulsion) or the injury lies more distally in the trunks. Branches that arise directly from the roots are tested: the dorsal scapular nerve (rhomboids) and the long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior, so winging of the scapula). Weakness of these, Horner's syndrome or a raised hemidiaphragm (phrenic, C3–C5, nearby) suggest a very proximal injury. Imaging and nerve conduction studies then define the level. Avulsion cannot recover spontaneously and has a worse prognosis, whereas a stretch injury of the trunks may recover partly over months.
questions.concept: Brachial plexus organisation explains Erb and Klumpke palsies.

questions.q: Which nerve supplies gluteus medius and gluteus minimus?
questions.why: The superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae, the main hip abductors.
optWhy: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus.
The femoral nerve supplies quadriceps and other anterior thigh muscles.
Correct: superior gluteal nerve.
The obturator nerve supplies the adductors.
questions.clue: 'Gluteus medius and minimus'.
questions.concept: Nerve supply of the hip abductors.

followUp.q: After a total hip replacement through a lateral approach, a patient's pelvis drops on the left when she stands on her right leg. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
followUp.why: Standing on the right leg relies on the right hip abductors to keep the left side of the pelvis up. The pelvis dropping on the left therefore indicates weak right abductors, supplied by the right superior gluteal nerve. The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, and the femoral nerve supplies knee extensors.

questions.q: A 45-year-old has a tight plaster cast below the knee removed and now cannot dorsiflex or evert the foot. The dorsum of the foot and lateral leg are numb. Inversion and plantarflexion are normal. Where is the lesion?
options: Common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula
Tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa
Deep fibular nerve alone in the anterior compartment
questions.why: Loss of dorsiflexion (deep fibular) and eversion (superficial fibular) with numbness of the lateral leg and dorsum indicates the common fibular nerve, which is superficial at the fibular neck where a cast can compress it. Normal inversion and plantarflexion show the tibial nerve is intact.
optWhy: Correct: common fibular nerve at the fibular neck.
A sciatic lesion would also weaken the hamstrings and tibial-supplied muscles.
An L5 lesion would also weaken inversion (tibialis posterior) and hip abduction.
The tibial nerve supplies plantarflexion and inversion, which are normal.
An isolated deep fibular lesion spares eversion and leaves only the first web space numb.
questions.clue: Cast at the knee, dorsiflexion and eversion lost, inversion normal.
questions.concept: Localising foot drop.

followUp.q: A 50-year-old has back pain and foot drop. Ankle inversion and hip abduction are also weak on that side, and the numbness covers the dorsum of the foot and big toe. What is the most likely lesion?
followUp.why: Weakness of dorsiflexion, inversion (tibialis posterior) and hip abduction (gluteus medius) spans the common fibular, tibial and superior gluteal nerves, which share the L5 root. A common fibular palsy spares inversion and abduction; S1 affects plantarflexion and the ankle jerk; the femoral nerve affects knee extension.

questions.q: An 82-year-old woman falls and her right leg is shortened and externally rotated. X-ray shows a displaced intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck. Why is replacement of the femoral head usually preferred to fixation?
options: The femoral head is supplied mainly by the obturator artery, which is torn
Fixation would damage the sciatic nerve
Bone in the neck cannot heal in older people
The retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery are likely torn, so the head may die or not unite
The lateral circumflex femoral artery supplies only the head
questions.why: The femoral head depends mainly on retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running up the neck within the capsule. Displacement tears them, so avascular necrosis and non-union are common after fixation; NICE CG124 recommends replacement arthroplasty for displaced intracapsular fractures.
optWhy: The artery of the ligament of the head (from the obturator) is small in adults and is not the main supply.
The sciatic nerve is not the reason for choosing arthroplasty.
Bone can heal in older people; the problem is the blood supply to the head.
Correct: loss of the retinacular supply makes the head unreliable after fixation.
The lateral circumflex femoral artery contributes less; the medial circumflex is the main supply.
questions.clue: Displaced intracapsular fracture in an older adult.
questions.concept: Blood supply of the femoral head determines treatment.

followUp.q: A 78-year-old has an intertrochanteric (extracapsular) fracture of the femur above the lesser trochanter that is not reverse oblique. According to NICE CG124, which implant is preferred?
followUp.why: Extracapsular trochanteric fractures keep the femoral head's blood supply, so the head is kept and the fracture fixed. NICE recommends an extramedullary implant such as a sliding hip screw in preference to an intramedullary nail for fractures above and including the lesser trochanter (except reverse oblique). Arthroplasty is for displaced intracapsular fractures; nails are for subtrochanteric fractures.

questions.q: A cardiologist needs arterial access in the groin for coronary angiography. Where should the femoral artery be palpated?
options: At the midpoint of the inguinal ligament
At the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis
Just lateral to the pubic tubercle
At the apex of the femoral triangle
questions.why: The femoral artery lies at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis, just below the inguinal ligament. The vein lies medial to it and the nerve lateral.
optWhy: The midpoint of the inguinal ligament (ASIS to pubic tubercle) marks the deep inguinal ring and lies slightly lateral.
Correct: mid-inguinal point.
Just lateral to the pubic tubercle lies the superficial ring and, below, the femoral canal region, medial to the artery.
The artery lies lateral, not medial, to the femoral vein.
At the apex the artery is deep under sartorius and passing into the adductor canal, which is not used for access.
questions.clue: 'Femoral artery' and 'groin'.
questions.concept: Surface marking of the femoral artery.

followUp.q: A clinician needs to cannulate the femoral vein. Relative to the palpable femoral pulse, where should the needle go?
followUp.why: From lateral to medial the femoral triangle contains nerve, artery, vein and canal, so the vein lies just medial to the arterial pulse below the inguinal ligament. Lateral to the pulse is the femoral nerve; above the ligament the vessels are external iliac and not accessible.

questions.q: List the contents of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial, state its boundaries, and give one clinical use of this arrangement.
markScheme: Boundaries: inguinal ligament (superior), medial border of sartorius (lateral), medial border of adductor longus (medial)
Floor: iliopsoas, pectineus, adductor longus; roof: fascia lata
Contents lateral to medial: femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, femoral canal (lymphatics, lymph node)
Femoral sheath encloses artery, vein and canal but not the nerve
Clinical use: femoral pulse at the mid-inguinal point for arterial access; vein just medial for venous access; femoral hernia through the canal
questions.modelAnswer: The femoral triangle lies in the upper anterior thigh. It is bounded above by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the medial border of sartorius and medially by the medial border of adductor longus; its floor is formed by iliopsoas, pectineus and adductor longus, and its roof by the fascia lata. From lateral to medial it contains the femoral nerve, the femoral artery, the femoral vein and the femoral canal, which holds lymphatics and a lymph node. The artery, vein and canal are wrapped in the femoral sheath; the nerve lies outside it. This fixed order is used clinically: the femoral pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point and gives arterial access for angiography, and the femoral vein can be found just medial to the pulse for venous access, while the nerve lies lateral. The femoral canal is the route of a femoral hernia, which appears below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
questions.concept: Ordered contents of the femoral triangle guide access.

questions.q:
An 81-year-old woman falls at home and cannot stand. Her right leg is shortened and externally rotated. X-ray shows a displaced intracapsular fracture of the right femoral neck. During her admission an intramuscular injection is given into the lower medial part of the right buttock, after which she reports numbness of the sole and weakness of knee flexion and all foot movements.

Explain the anatomy behind the leg's position and the choice of surgical treatment for her fracture. Then identify the nerve likely to have been injured by the injection, describe the expected deficits, and explain how intramuscular gluteal injections should be given to avoid this.
markScheme: Shortening: muscles crossing the hip (gluteals, hamstrings, adductors, rectus femoris) pull the distal fragment upwards
External rotation: iliopsoas on the lesser trochanter and short lateral rotators turn the shaft outwards once the neck is broken
Femoral head supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running up the neck within the capsule; artery of ligament of head contributes little in adults
Displaced intracapsular fracture tears these vessels: risk of avascular necrosis and non-union; so replacement arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or THR for selected people) per NICE CG124
Extracapsular fractures keep blood supply and are fixed (sliding hip screw for most trochanteric fractures)
Injection injury: sciatic nerve (L4–S3), passing below piriformis through the lower medial buttock

Deficits: weak knee flexion (hamstrings), paralysis of all muscles below the knee (tibial and common fibular), sensory loss below the knee except medial leg (saphenous), absent ankle jerk; knee extension and adduction spared
Safe site: upper outer quadrant of the buttock or the ventrogluteal site in gluteus medius
questions.concept: Femoral head blood supply and the course of the sciatic nerve.

questions.q: Which structure passes through the foramen spinosum?
questions.why: The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, enters the middle cranial fossa through the foramen spinosum.
optWhy: V3 passes through the foramen ovale.
V2 passes through the foramen rotundum.
Correct: the middle meningeal artery.
The internal carotid enters via the carotid canal.
questions.clue: 'Foramen spinosum'.
questions.concept: Contents of the skull foramina.

followUp.q: Which nerve passes through the foramen ovale?
followUp.why: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) passes through the foramen ovale. V2 uses the foramen rotundum, VII the internal acoustic meatus, and VI the superior orbital fissure.

questions.q: A 19-year-old is hit on the side of the head by a cricket ball. He is briefly knocked out, then talks normally for an hour before becoming drowsy, with a dilating left pupil. CT shows a lens-shaped hyperdense collection over the left temporal lobe that does not cross suture lines. Which vessel is most likely bleeding?
questions.why: A biconvex collection limited by sutures after a temporal blow is an extradural haematoma, usually from a branch of the middle meningeal artery torn by a fracture near the pterion. The arterial bleed expands quickly between the skull and dura.
optWhy: Bridging veins cause subdural haematomas, which are crescentic and cross sutures.
Middle cerebral artery bleeding is intracerebral or subarachnoid, not extradural.
Correct: middle meningeal artery bleeding gives an extradural haematoma.
Sagittal sinus injury is midline and venous, not a temporal lens-shaped collection.
Anterior communicating aneurysm rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage.
questions.clue: Temporal blow, lucid interval, lens-shaped collection not crossing sutures.
questions.concept: Extradural haematoma anatomy.

followUp.q: An 84-year-old on an anticoagulant becomes increasingly confused over two weeks after a minor fall. CT shows a crescent-shaped collection over the right hemisphere crossing suture lines. What is the source of bleeding?
followUp.why: A crescentic collection crossing sutures is a subdural haematoma from bridging veins crossing the subdural space; brain atrophy in older people stretches these veins. Middle meningeal bleeding is extradural; an aneurysm bleeds into the subarachnoid space; the choroid plexus is intraventricular.

questions.q: A 60-year-old has sudden weakness of the lower half of the right side of the face and a weak right arm. She can wrinkle both sides of her forehead. Where is the lesion?
options: Left motor cortex or its descending fibres
Right facial nerve in the facial canal
Left facial nucleus in the pons
questions.why: Lower facial weakness with forehead sparing and weakness of the arm on the same side indicates an upper motor neuron lesion in the opposite (left) hemisphere, such as a stroke. The forehead is spared because its motor neurons receive input from both hemispheres.
optWhy: Correct: left upper motor neuron lesion.
A right facial nerve lesion is lower motor neuron and weakens the whole right face including the forehead.
A parotid lesion affects the facial nerve branches (lower motor neuron) and would not weaken the arm.
A cerebellopontine angle lesion would cause lower motor neuron weakness, often with hearing loss.
A left facial nucleus lesion would weaken the left, not right, face.
questions.clue: Forehead spared, arm weak on the same side.
questions.concept: Upper versus lower motor neuron facial weakness.

followUp.q: A man has right facial weakness including the forehead, with normal taste, normal tearing and no hyperacusis. A firm lump is felt in front of the right ear. Where is the lesion most likely?
options: Right facial nerve at or distal to the stylomastoid foramen, in the parotid
followUp.why: Whole-face weakness is lower motor neuron; sparing of taste, tearing and stapedius means the branches inside the canal are intact, so the lesion is beyond the stylomastoid foramen, here in the parotid. A cortical lesion spares the forehead; lesions at the geniculate ganglion or internal acoustic meatus would affect tearing, taste and stapedius.

questions.q: On the first day after a total thyroidectomy, a 45-year-old woman has a hoarse, breathy voice. Which nerve has most likely been injured, and where?
options: External laryngeal nerve near the superior thyroid artery
Recurrent laryngeal nerve in the tracheo-oesophageal groove near the inferior thyroid artery
questions.why: A hoarse, breathy voice indicates a weak vocal fold from injury to one recurrent laryngeal nerve, which supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid and runs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove close to the inferior thyroid artery.
optWhy: External laryngeal injury weakens cricothyroid, causing loss of high pitch and voice fatigue rather than a breathy, hoarse voice.
The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies stylopharyngeus and pharyngeal sensation.
The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue and is not near the thyroid lobes.
Correct: unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
Phrenic injury paralyses a hemidiaphragm, not the voice.
questions.clue: Hoarse breathy voice after thyroidectomy.
questions.concept: Recurrent laryngeal nerve supply and course.

followUp.q: A soprano notices she can no longer reach high notes after thyroid surgery, although her speaking voice is normal. Which nerve was most likely damaged?
followUp.why: The external laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal folds for high pitch; it runs with the superior thyroid artery. The recurrent laryngeal nerve controls the other intrinsic muscles (hoarseness), the internal laryngeal nerve is sensory above the folds, and a vagal lesion would cause wider deficits.

questions.q: State the boundaries of the posterior triangle of the neck, name two important contents, and explain the effect of injury to the accessory nerve there.
markScheme: Anterior: posterior border of sternocleidomastoid; posterior: anterior border of trapezius; inferior: middle third of the clavicle
Roof: investing layer of deep cervical fascia; floor: prevertebral fascia over the scalenes, levator scapulae and splenius
Contents include the accessory nerve, the trunks of the brachial plexus, the subclavian artery (third part), external jugular vein and lymph nodes
Accessory nerve runs superficially across the triangle and is vulnerable in node biopsy
Injury weakens trapezius: shoulder droop, weak shoulder shrug and difficulty abducting the arm above 90°
questions.modelAnswer: The posterior triangle of the neck is bounded in front by the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid, behind by the anterior border of trapezius and below by the middle third of the clavicle. Its roof is the investing layer of deep cervical fascia and its floor the prevertebral fascia over the scalene, levator scapulae and splenius muscles. Important contents include the accessory nerve (XI), the trunks of the brachial plexus, the third part of the subclavian artery, the external jugular vein and lymph nodes. The accessory nerve crosses the triangle superficially, just under the investing fascia, so it is easily cut during lymph node biopsy. Injury paralyses trapezius, causing drooping of the shoulder, a weak shoulder shrug and difficulty raising the arm above the horizontal, because trapezius helps rotate the scapula during abduction.
questions.concept: Superficial course of the accessory nerve in the posterior triangle.

questions.q: 'The thyroid gland is the most dangerous organ in the neck for a surgeon, not because of its own structure, but because of what lies around it.' Discuss this statement with reference to the embryology, blood supply, relations and nerve supply of the thyroid and parathyroid glands, and the complications that follow thyroidectomy.
markScheme: Embryology: thyroid from the foramen caecum, descends along the thyroglossal duct (remnants form midline cysts that rise on tongue protrusion)
Parathyroids: inferior from the third pouch (migrate with thymus, variable position), superior from the fourth pouch (more constant)
Relations: within pretracheal fascia (moves on swallowing); isthmus over upper tracheal rings; lobes against larynx, trachea, oesophagus; carotid sheath laterally
Blood supply: superior thyroid artery (external carotid), inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk), occasional thyroid ima; veins to IJV and brachiocephalic
External laryngeal nerve with superior thyroid artery: cricothyroid, high pitch
Recurrent laryngeal nerve in tracheo-oesophageal groove close to inferior thyroid artery: unilateral injury hoarseness, bilateral stridor and airway risk
Parathyroid devascularisation or removal: hypocalcaemia (perioral tingling, tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs)
Haematoma under pretracheal fascia can compress the airway; gland's own features (retrosternal goitre, vascular gland, malignancy) also add risk; balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement captures a real surgical truth but understates the thyroid's own contribution to risk.

Embryology explains much of the danger. The thyroid begins at the foramen caecum of the tongue and descends along the thyroglossal duct to the front of the neck; remnants form midline cysts that rise on tongue protrusion. The parathyroids come from the pharyngeal pouches: the superior pair from the fourth pouch stays fairly constant near the back of the gland, while the inferior pair from the third pouch migrates with the thymus and may lie anywhere from the jaw angle to the mediastinum, making them harder to find and protect.

The gland lies within the pretracheal fascia, so it moves on swallowing, with its isthmus over the upper tracheal rings and its lobes against the larynx, trachea and oesophagus; the carotid sheath lies laterally. It is supplied by the superior thyroid artery (the first branch of the external carotid) and the inferior thyroid artery (from the thyrocervical trunk), with an occasional thyroid ima artery, and drained by superior, middle and inferior thyroid veins. Bleeding inside the closed fascial compartment can compress the airway, so a tense post-operative neck haematoma is an emergency.

The nerves at risk:
- The external laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery. Injury paralyses cricothyroid, causing loss of high pitch and voice fatigue; ligating the artery close to the gland protects it.
- The recurrent laryngeal nerve climbs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove close to branches of the inferior thyroid artery. It supplies all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles, so injury to one nerve causes hoarseness, and injury to both can leave the vocal folds near the midline, with stridor and airway obstruction.

The parathyroids receive most of their blood from the inferior thyroid artery. Removing them or cutting off their blood supply causes hypocalcaemia, with perioral tingling, tetany and Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs; it is a common significant complication after total thyroidectomy and is often temporary.

The gland's own features also matter: a retrosternal goitre, a very vascular gland in Graves' disease or an invasive cancer makes surgery harder, and total thyroidectomy inevitably causes hypothyroidism that needs lifelong replacement.

In conclusion, most serious complications do arise from neighbouring structures whose positions follow from development. Careful identification of the nerves and parathyroids, often with nerve monitoring, is the core of safe thyroid surgery, but the statement overlooks the real contribution of the gland's own pathology.
questions.concept: Thyroid relations, embryology and nerves at risk.

questions.q: Which pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands?
questions.why: The third pouch gives the inferior parathyroids (dorsal part) and thymus (ventral part). They migrate further than the superior glands, ending below them.
optWhy: The first pouch forms the middle ear and auditory tube.
The second forms the lining of the palatine tonsil.
Correct: third pouch.
The fourth forms the superior parathyroids and C cells.
questions.clue: 'Inferior parathyroid'.
questions.concept: Pharyngeal pouch derivatives.

followUp.q: During thyroidectomy a surgeon cannot find one inferior parathyroid gland in its usual place. Where is it most likely to be found?
options: Near or within the thymus in the superior mediastinum
followUp.why: The inferior parathyroids develop from the third pouch with the thymus and can be carried down with it, so ectopic glands are often in or near the thymus in the superior mediastinum. The middle ear and tonsil are first and second pouch derivatives.

questions.q: A baby with Down syndrome is born with a midline defect at the umbilicus. Bowel and liver protrude inside a translucent membrane into which the umbilical cord inserts. What is the developmental explanation?
options: A defect beside the umbilicus with no covering sac
Failure of the urachus to close
Failure of the physiological midgut herniation to return to the abdomen
questions.why: This is an omphalocele: the midgut normally herniates into the cord around week 6 and returns by about week 10. Failure to return leaves gut (and sometimes liver) in a membrane-covered sac at the umbilicus. Omphalocele is often associated with other anomalies, including chromosomal ones.
optWhy: Malrotation affects position and fixation of gut inside the abdomen; it does not create a covered sac.
This describes gastroschisis, which has no covering sac and lies beside the umbilicus.
Vitelline duct remnants give a Meckel's diverticulum or umbilical fistula, not a covered sac of bowel and liver.
A patent urachus leaks urine from the umbilicus.
Correct: persistent physiological herniation gives a covered midline defect.
questions.clue: Midline, covered by membrane, cord inserts into the sac.
questions.concept: Physiological herniation and omphalocele.

followUp.q: A newborn has loops of bowel lying free, without any covering, through a small defect just to the right of a normal umbilical cord. What is this?
followUp.why: Uncovered bowel beside a normally inserted cord is gastroschisis. An omphalocele is covered and midline with the cord inserting into it; an umbilical hernia is skin-covered; a patent urachus leaks urine.

questions.q: A newborn is cyanosed. Echocardiography shows a ventricular septal defect, an aorta overriding the septum, narrowing of the right ventricular outflow tract and right ventricular hypertrophy. Why is the baby cyanosed?
options: Blood shunts left to right through the VSD
The ductus arteriosus has closed early
Outflow obstruction diverts deoxygenated right ventricular blood through the VSD into the overriding aorta
The foramen ovale has failed to close
The pulmonary veins drain to the right atrium
questions.why: In tetralogy of Fallot, the narrowed right ventricular outflow raises right-sided pressure, so deoxygenated blood passes through the VSD into the aorta, which overrides the septum. Desaturated blood reaching the systemic circulation causes cyanosis.
optWhy: A left-to-right shunt sends oxygenated blood to the lungs and does not cause cyanosis.
Ductal closure matters in some duct-dependent lesions but does not explain the four features described.
Correct: right-to-left flow into the overriding aorta.
A patent foramen ovale is common and not the defect described.
Anomalous pulmonary venous drainage is a different lesion.
questions.clue: VSD, overriding aorta, outflow stenosis, RVH, cyanosis.
questions.concept: Tetralogy of Fallot causes a right-to-left shunt.

followUp.q: Which fetal structure carries blood from the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta, bypassing the lungs?
followUp.why: The ductus arteriosus links the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. The ductus venosus bypasses the liver, the foramen ovale links the atria, and the umbilical arteries return blood to the placenta.

questions.q: A woman planning a pregnancy asks when folic acid should be started to reduce the risk of spina bifida. Which answer best reflects NHS advice and the embryology?
options: Start before conception, ideally about three months before, and continue for the first 12 weeks
Start only after the first missed period is confirmed by scan at 12 weeks
Take it only in the third trimester
Folic acid has no role in neural tube defects
questions.why: The neural tube closes by about day 28 after conception, often before a pregnancy is recognised. NHS advice is to start folic acid before pregnancy, ideally about three months before, or as soon as pregnant, and continue for the first 12 weeks.
optWhy: Correct: start before conception and continue to 12 weeks.
By 20 weeks the neural tube closed months earlier.
Starting at 12 weeks misses the window of neural tube closure.
The third trimester is far too late for neural tube closure.
Low folate is a recognised risk factor and supplementation reduces risk.
questions.clue: 'Planning a pregnancy' and 'spina bifida'.
questions.concept: Timing of neural tube closure and folic acid advice.

followUp.q: At about which day after conception does the caudal neuropore normally close?
followUp.why: The cranial neuropore closes at about day 25 and the caudal at about day 28. Day 7 is around implantation, day 14 is the bilaminar disc stage, and by day 60 the embryonic period is ending.

questions.q: Describe the three shunts in the fetal circulation, explain why each is needed, and state what each becomes after birth.
markScheme: Ductus venosus: umbilical vein blood bypasses the liver to the IVC; becomes ligamentum venosum (umbilical vein becomes ligamentum teres)
Foramen ovale: right atrium to left atrium, sending oxygenated IVC blood to the left heart and brain; becomes fossa ovalis
Ductus arteriosus: pulmonary trunk to descending aorta, bypassing high-resistance fluid-filled lungs; becomes ligamentum arteriosum
Shunts are needed because the placenta, not the lungs, oxygenates blood and pulmonary resistance is high
At birth lung expansion lowers pulmonary resistance; left atrial pressure rises and closes the foramen ovale flap
Ductus arteriosus constricts after birth; ductus venosus closes when umbilical flow stops
questions.modelAnswer: Before birth the placenta oxygenates the blood and the fluid-filled lungs have a high resistance, so three shunts direct blood away from the liver and lungs. The ductus venosus carries oxygen-rich blood from the umbilical vein past the liver into the inferior vena cava; it becomes the ligamentum venosum, and the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres. In the right atrium, much of this blood crosses the foramen ovale into the left atrium, so the best-oxygenated blood reaches the left ventricle, the heart and the brain; the foramen becomes the fossa ovalis. Blood that does enter the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk is largely diverted through the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta, bypassing the lungs; it becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. At birth, the lungs expand and pulmonary resistance falls, so far more blood returns to the left atrium, raising its pressure above the right and pushing the flap of the foramen ovale closed. The ductus arteriosus constricts over the following hours to days, and the ductus venosus closes once umbilical flow stops.
questions.concept: The fetal shunts and their closure at birth.

cases.title: Back pain that became an emergency

steps.text: A 39-year-old delivery driver sees his GP with five days of low back pain and pain radiating down both legs, worse on the right. He has been taking simple painkillers.

ask.q: Which question is most important to ask next?
options: Whether he has any change in bladder, bowel or sexual function or numbness around the anus or genitals
Whether he has had back pain before
Whether his job involves heavy lifting
ask.why: Pain in both legs raises concern about central compression of the cauda equina, so the sacral-root symptoms (bladder, bowel, sexual function, saddle sensation) must be asked about directly. Previous episodes, analgesia and occupation are part of a full history but do not change the urgency.

steps.text: He admits that for the last day he has had to strain to start passing urine and that toilet paper 'feels strange' when he wipes. On examination there is reduced pinprick sensation around the anus and weak ankle plantarflexion on both sides.

ask.q: Which roots are responsible for the altered perianal sensation?
ask.why: The perianal and perineal (saddle) skin is supplied by S2–S5, the lowest roots of the cauda equina. L1–L2 supply the groin and upper thigh, L4–L5 the leg and foot, and T11–T12 the lower abdominal wall.

steps.text: The GP suspects cauda equina syndrome. A practice nurse offers to do a bladder scan first to 'see whether he really needs hospital'.

ask.q: What is the most appropriate action?
options: Emergency referral to hospital for MRI now
Arrange a routine MRI through the community
Do the bladder scan and refer only if the residual volume is high
Start physiotherapy and review in a week
ask.why: Recent-onset urinary hesitancy and saddle numbness with leg pain are red flags. The England pathway asks for emergency referral and MRI as soon as possible (within four hours of request) and says a bladder scan must not decide alone. Routine imaging or physiotherapy would delay decompression.

steps.text: Outcome: MRI shows a large central L4/L5 disc prolapse compressing the cauda equina. He has urgent surgical decompression and, with early treatment, regains bladder control.

debrief: Pain in both legs or any bladder, bowel, sexual or saddle-sensation change in someone with back pain means asking directly about sacral-root function.
Saddle sensation is S2–S5; these roots also control the bladder and bowel.
Suspected cauda equina syndrome needs emergency MRI; a bladder scan alone should not decide the referral.
A central prolapse can compress several roots of the cauda equina at once, unlike the single-root picture of a posterolateral prolapse.

cases.title: Tingling hand at night

steps.text: A 50-year-old warehouse supervisor has three months of tingling in her right hand that wakes her at night. She shakes the hand to relieve it.

ask.q: Which detail of the history would best help localise the nerve involved?
ask.why: The distribution of tingling separates median (thumb, index, middle and lateral half of ring), ulnar (little and medial half of ring) and root (dermatomal) lesions. Handedness, alcohol and neck stiffness may be relevant later but localise less.

steps.text: She points to her thumb, index and middle fingers. On examination there is mild wasting of the thenar eminence and weak thumb abduction. Sensation over the thenar eminence itself is normal. Tapping over the front of the wrist reproduces the tingling.

ask.q: Why is thenar skin sensation normal?
options: The thenar skin is supplied by the radial nerve
The ulnar nerve supplies the thenar skin
The palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
ask.why: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves before the wrist and runs superficial to the retinaculum, outside the tunnel. Tingling in the digits shows sensory fibres in the tunnel are affected; the radial and ulnar nerves do not supply the thenar palm.

steps.text: Her triceps and biceps reflexes are normal and neck movements do not reproduce the symptoms. Nerve conduction studies show slowed median nerve conduction across the wrist.

ask.q: Which structure forms the roof of the tunnel compressing the nerve?
ask.why: The carpal tunnel is roofed by the flexor retinaculum, stretched between the scaphoid and trapezium laterally and the hamate and pisiform medially. The palmar aponeurosis is more superficial; the extensor retinaculum is on the back of the wrist; the pisohamate ligament forms part of Guyon's canal.

steps.text: Outcome: carpal tunnel syndrome is diagnosed. Management is discussed with her, ranging from wrist splinting at night to surgical release of the flexor retinaculum if symptoms persist or wasting progresses.

debrief: The distribution of sensory symptoms is the quickest way to localise a hand nerve lesion.
Sparing of thenar skin is a classic clue that the median nerve is compressed in the carpal tunnel rather than higher up.
Normal reflexes and a non-dermatomal pattern argue against a cervical root lesion.
The tunnel contains the median nerve and nine flexor tendons under the flexor retinaculum.

cases.title: Hit by a cricket ball

steps.text: A 19-year-old is struck on the right side of the head just above the zygomatic arch by a cricket ball. He is knocked out for about a minute, then gets up, says he feels fine and talks normally.

ask.q: Why is the site of this blow a particular concern?
options: It overlies the superior sagittal sinus
It is near the pterion, where thin bone overlies a branch of the middle meningeal artery
It overlies the cavernous sinus directly
ask.why: The pterion lies on the side of the skull above the zygomatic arch, where frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid meet. The bone is thin and overlies a branch of the middle meningeal artery. The sagittal sinus is midline, the occipital lobe posterior and the cavernous sinus deep beside the sphenoid body.

steps.text: Ninety minutes later he becomes drowsy and confused and vomits. His right pupil is larger than the left and reacts sluggishly.

ask.q: Which best explains the enlarging right pupil?
options: Compression of the right oculomotor nerve by the medial temporal lobe pushed down by the expanding clot
Direct injury to the right optic nerve
ask.why: An expanding supratentorial clot pushes the medial temporal lobe (uncus) through the tentorial notch, compressing the oculomotor nerve on the same side. Its parasympathetic pupillary fibres lie on the outside of the nerve, so the pupil dilates early. Optic nerve injury causes an afferent defect, not this picture; abducens palsy affects eye abduction, not the pupil.

steps.text: CT head shows a biconvex hyperdense collection over the right temporal lobe that does not cross the coronal or lambdoid sutures, with a fracture of the squamous temporal bone.

ask.q: Between which layers has the blood collected?
options: Between the dura and the arachnoid
Between the skull and the dura
ask.why: A biconvex collection limited by sutures is an extradural haematoma, lying between the skull and the dura, which is firmly attached at the sutures. Subdural blood (dura–arachnoid) is crescentic and crosses sutures; subarachnoid blood outlines sulci and cisterns; parenchymal blood lies within the brain.

steps.text: Outcome: he has emergency neurosurgical evacuation of the haematoma and makes a good recovery.

debrief: A blow over the pterion can tear a branch of the middle meningeal artery, which runs between the skull and the dura.
A lucid interval occurs in only a minority of extradural haematomas, so its absence does not exclude one.
A dilating pupil on the side of the clot signals compression of the oculomotor nerve by herniating temporal lobe.
Extradural haematomas are lens-shaped and limited by sutures; subdural haematomas are crescentic and can cross them.

osce.title: Upper limb neurological examination
steps: Clean your hands, introduce yourself, confirm the patient's identity, explain the examination, gain consent and ask about pain
Expose the arms and shoulders appropriately and position the patient sitting comfortably
Inspect for wasting (e.g. thenar or interossei), fasciculation, tremor, scars and posture; note aids or splints nearby
Ask the patient to hold the arms out with palms up and eyes closed to look for pronator drift
Assess tone at the shoulder, elbow and wrist on each side

Test power one side at a time and grade with the MRC scale: shoulder abduction (C5), elbow flexion (C5/6), elbow extension (C7), wrist extension (C6), finger extension (C7), finger abduction and thumb abduction (T1)
Test reflexes: biceps (C5/6), supinator (C5/6) and triceps (C7), using reinforcement if absent
Assess coordination with finger–nose testing and rapid alternating movements
Test light touch and pinprick in each dermatome (C5–T1) and in peripheral nerve areas, then vibration and joint position sense
Thank the patient, clean your hands and summarise findings, suggesting whether the pattern fits a root, plexus, peripheral nerve or upper motor neuron lesion
tips: Compare sides at every step: asymmetry is often the key finding.
Distinguish dermatomes (roots) from peripheral nerve territories when mapping sensory loss.
Follow your own medical school's mark scheme where its order differs.
Present positives first, then relevant negatives, then your localisation.

interpret.title: CSF from a lumbar puncture
rows: about 60% or more of blood glucose
interpret.q: A lumbar puncture is performed at L3/L4 in a 30-year-old with headache. (Ranges are typical adult values and vary by laboratory.) What do these CSF results show?
interpret.why: Every value is within the typical range: clear fluid, fewer than 5 white cells, no red cells, protein 0.35 g/L and a CSF:blood glucose ratio of 3.6 ÷ 5.5 ≈ 0.65 (65%). The needle has reached the subarachnoid space of the lumbar cistern and obtained normal CSF.
optWhy: Bacterial meningitis gives a high neutrophil count, high protein and a low glucose ratio (often below about 40%).
Correct: all values are typical, with a glucose ratio of about 0.65.
Viral meningitis gives a raised lymphocyte count with normal or mildly raised protein.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage gives red cells and, after some hours, xanthochromia.
A traumatic tap introduces red cells, usually falling from the first to the last sample.

interpret.title: Inferior territory on a lead II strip
interpret.q: A 68-year-old has 40 minutes of crushing central chest pain. The lead II strip (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV) is regular with a P before every QRS; the R–R interval is 30 small squares, the PR 4.5 small squares and the ST segment is raised 2 mm. Leads III and aVF show similar ST elevation and leads I and aVL show ST depression. She is known to have a right-dominant circulation. Which is the best interpretation?
options: Sinus bradycardia at 50/min with ST depression from subendocardial ischaemia
Sinus rhythm at 100/min with anterior ST elevation from the left anterior descending artery
First-degree heart block with lateral ST elevation from the circumflex artery
Sinus bradycardia at 50/min with inferior ST elevation, most likely right coronary artery occlusion
Complete heart block with inferior ST elevation
interpret.why: R–R = 30 × 0.04 s = 1.2 s, so the rate is 60/1.2 = 50/min (1,500 ÷ 30): sinus bradycardia. PR = 4.5 × 0.04 = 0.18 s, within the normal 0.12–0.20 s. ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL shows inferior infarction; in a right-dominant heart the inferior wall and usually the SA node are supplied by the right coronary artery.
optWhy: The ST segment is raised in lead II, not depressed; depression appears only in the reciprocal leads I and aVL.
100/min would need an R–R of 15 small squares; and the changes are in the inferior, not anterior, leads.
First-degree block needs a PR over 0.20 s (more than 5 small squares); 0.18 s is normal, and the elevation is inferior, not lateral.
Correct: rate 50/min, normal PR, inferior ST elevation in a right-dominant heart points to the RCA.
Complete heart block shows P waves unrelated to QRS complexes; here a P precedes every QRS with a constant PR.

interpret.title: Observations after a chest stab wound
rows: typically 95 or above on air in healthy adults
systolic roughly 100–140 in a healthy young adult
JVP normally not visibly raised when sitting at 45°
interpret.q: A 23-year-old has these findings 10 minutes after a stab wound to the left chest (ranges are typical adult values and vary). What is the most likely cause of his low blood pressure?
options: Reduced venous return from a left tension pneumothorax
Haemorrhage into the left pleural space
interpret.why: Hyperresonance with absent breath sounds shows air in the left pleural space, and tracheal deviation away from that side shows mediastinal shift. Distended neck veins with hypotension mean venous return to the heart is obstructed, which is the haemodynamic effect of a tension pneumothorax.
optWhy: Correct: air under tension shifts the mediastinum and impairs venous return.
Blood in the pleura would be dull to percussion, and haemorrhage gives flat neck veins.
Tamponade raises the JVP but does not make one hemithorax hyperresonant or shift the trachea.
Sepsis does not develop within minutes of a wound and would not explain the chest signs.
Neurogenic shock gives hypotension with a slow heart rate, not tachycardia and unilateral chest signs.

interpret.title: Jaundice after biliary colic
interpret.q: A 48-year-old woman with known gallstones has three days of jaundice, pale stools and dark urine. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct. (Ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.) Which interpretation best fits these results?
options: Hepatocellular injury, for example viral hepatitis
Obstruction of the common bile duct, most likely by a stone
Chronic liver failure with low synthetic function
interpret.why: ALP is four times the upper limit (520 vs 130) while ALT is only about twice it (92 vs 40), with a raised bilirubin, pale stools and dark urine: a cholestatic (obstructive) pattern. A dilated common bile duct places the block below the confluence of the hepatic ducts, and a stone from the gallbladder passing down the cystic duct is the commonest cause.
optWhy: Hepatitis raises ALT much more than ALP, often into the hundreds or thousands.
Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, so the urine is not dark with bilirubin and the ALP is normal.
Correct: cholestatic pattern with a dilated duct indicates obstruction, usually a stone.
Amylase is normal, so there is no evidence of pancreatitis at present, though a stone at the ampulla can cause it.
Albumin is normal, so synthetic function is preserved.

interpret.title: Kidney function after pelvic surgery
interpret.q: A 46-year-old woman had a total abdominal hysterectomy. On day 3 she has left loin pain and her urine output is adequate. Ultrasound shows a dilated left renal pelvis and ureter down to the pelvis; the right kidney is normal. (Ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.) What is the most likely explanation?
options: Pre-renal acute kidney injury from blood loss
Urinary retention from bladder outlet obstruction
Left ureteric injury or ligation near the uterine artery
interpret.why: Creatinine has more than doubled (68 to 152 µmol/L, a 2.2-fold rise) with unilateral hydronephrosis and loin pain on the operated side. A dilated ureter all the way down to the pelvis places the block where the ureter passes beneath the uterine artery beside the cervix, a recognised site of injury in hysterectomy.
optWhy: Pre-renal injury would not dilate one renal pelvis and ureter, and haemoglobin is only mildly low.
A 2.2-fold creatinine rise with hydronephrosis is never a normal post-operative finding.
Tubular necrosis affects both kidneys and does not cause hydronephrosis.
Bladder outlet obstruction would dilate both upper tracts and distend the bladder.
Correct: unilateral hydroureteronephrosis to the pelvis after hysterectomy points to ureteric injury.

interpret.title: Bloods in a patient with carpal tunnel symptoms
interpret.q: A 54-year-old woman with bilateral carpal tunnel symptoms has also noticed tiredness, weight gain and feeling cold. (Ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.) What do these results suggest?
options: Primary hypothyroidism, a recognised association of carpal tunnel syndrome
interpret.why: A high TSH (14.6 mU/L) with a low free T4 (7.5 pmol/L) is primary hypothyroidism: the failing thyroid makes too little hormone and the pituitary responds by raising TSH. Hypothyroidism can cause soft-tissue swelling within the carpal tunnel, compressing the median nerve, and fits her other symptoms. HbA1c is normal, so diabetes, another association, is not present.
optWhy: HbA1c is 38 mmol/mol, below the usual diabetes threshold.
Correct: raised TSH and low free T4 indicate primary hypothyroidism.
Secondary hypothyroidism gives a low free T4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH, not a high TSH.
Hyperthyroidism gives a suppressed TSH and raised free T4.
TSH and free T4 are both outside their typical ranges.

interpret.title: Pre-operative bloods after hip fracture
interpret.q: An 82-year-old woman with a displaced intracapsular hip fracture had a haemoglobin of 121 g/L at a clinic visit last month. These are her admission bloods. (Ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.) Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: She has severe hyperkalaemia needing urgent treatment
She has hypercalcaemia suggesting a pathological fracture
Her results are all within normal limits
The fall in haemoglobin is expected blood loss into the thigh around the fracture, and she is mildly dehydrated
The low haemoglobin proves a gastrointestinal bleed
interpret.why: Haemoglobin has fallen by 17 g/L (121 to 104) since last month; hip fractures commonly bleed into the surrounding tissues. A urea rise (9.8) proportionally greater than the creatinine rise (98), with mild hyponatraemia, fits dehydration after a long lie, which needs correction before surgery.
optWhy: Potassium is 4.2 mmol/L, which is normal.
Adjusted calcium is 2.34 mmol/L, within the typical range, so there is no hypercalcaemia.
Haemoglobin, sodium, urea and creatinine are all outside the typical ranges.
Correct: fracture-related blood loss and dehydration explain the pattern.
Bleeding around the fracture is the likelier cause; nothing here points to the gut.

interpret.title: Bloods the day after thyroidectomy
interpret.q: The day after a total thyroidectomy, a 52-year-old woman has tingling around her mouth and in her fingers. (Ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.) What is the most likely explanation?
options: Hypoparathyroidism from removal or devascularisation of the parathyroid glands
interpret.why: Calcium is low (1.86 mmol/L) and phosphate is high, with an inappropriately low PTH (0.6 pmol/L): the pattern of hypoparathyroidism. The parathyroids sit on the back of the thyroid and get most of their blood from the inferior thyroid artery, so they can be removed or devascularised during total thyroidectomy. Perioral and finger tingling are early signs of hypocalcaemia.
optWhy: Correct: low calcium, high phosphate and low PTH point to hypoparathyroidism after surgery.
Vitamin D deficiency lowers calcium but PTH rises in response, and phosphate is usually low or normal.
Primary hyperparathyroidism gives high calcium and high PTH.
Magnesium is 0.82 mmol/L, within range, so it does not explain the hypocalcaemia.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness, not biochemical change or tingling.
